Autonomic (sympathetic/enteric) neurons are direct derivatives of trunk neural crest cells, which delaminate from the dorsal neural tube and migrate ventrally to form the sympathoadrenal and autonomic ganglion lineages, so both cell types descend from a common trunk neural-crest progenitor pool.

type:Autonomic progenitor.name: Autonomic progenitor
type:Autonomic progenitor.description: Autonomic progenitors are neural crest-derived precursor cells that give rise to the neurons and glia of the autonomic nervous system, including the sympathetic, parasympathetic, and enteric divisions. Emerging at E9.5–E10.0 as migrating neural crest cells coalesce at sites of future ganglia, these progenitors undergo specification toward autonomic fates and begin exiting the cell cycle to initiate neuronal differentiation.

topLinks.explanation: Autonomic progenitors are direct descendants of neural crest, and vagal (post-otic) neural crest is a well-established source of autonomic (parasympathetic/enteric and sympathoadrenal) neurons via a shared SOX10+/PHOX2B+ crest-derived progenitor pool, so the two cell types lie on the same delaminating-crest-to-autonomic-neuron lineage.

Autonomic neurons are the direct differentiated progeny of autonomic progenitors—both derive from the neural crest/sympathoadrenal lineage (e.g., trunk neural crest–derived sympathoblasts), so the progenitor-to-neuron transition within a single clone produces their strong shared ancestry.

Autonomic progenitors and dorsal root ganglion neurons both descend from trunk neural crest cells, which delaminate from the dorsal neural tube and generate both autonomic (sympathetic/parasympathetic) and sensory (DRG) lineages, so their linkage reflects a shared multipotent neural crest progenitor pool.

Both autonomic (sympathetic/parasympathetic) and dorsal root ganglion sensory progenitors are derived from a common pool of trunk neural crest cells that delaminate from the dorsal neural tube and migrate ventrally, so their shared ancestry reflects this single multipotent neural crest origin.

Trunk neural crest cells migrating ventrally along the sympathoadrenal pathway are the direct progenitors of autonomic (sympathetic) neurons, so the two cell types are sequential stages of a single neural-crest-derived lineage sharing a common recent progenitor pool.

type:Cranial neural crest.name: Cranial neural crest
type:Cranial neural crest.description: Cranial neural crest cells are a migratory population of ectoderm-derived cells that originate from the dorsal neural tube in the head region. They delaminate and migrate extensively to give rise to craniofacial cartilage and bone, cranial ganglia, smooth muscle, and connective tissue of the face and pharyngeal arches. This population is one of the largest neural crest subsets and is essential for building the vertebrate head.

topLinks.explanation: Cranial (particularly the trigeminal-level) neural crest is the direct progenitor of the neurons of the trigeminal ganglion, so the two cell types share ancestry because the ganglion neurons delaminate and differentiate directly from cranial neural crest cells (with an additional contribution from trigeminal placodes).

Cranial neural crest cells delaminate from the dorsal neural folds and migrate ventrally into the pharyngeal arches where they form the ectomesenchyme, so pharyngeal arch mesenchyme is largely a direct descendant of cranial neural crest, giving them a shared progenitor origin.

Cranial neural crest and roof plate both originate from the dorsal neuroepithelium/neural plate border of the anterior neural tube, where premigratory neural crest delaminates from the same dorsal progenitors that give rise to the roof plate, so they share recent common ancestors in this dorsal neural progenitor pool.

Frontonasal mesenchyme is largely populated by cranial (frontonasal-prominence) neural crest cells that delaminate from the anterior neural folds and migrate ventrally, so both cell types descend from a shared cranial neural crest progenitor pool.

Both are neural crest populations delaminating from the dorsal neural folds/neural plate border, differing only in anteroposterior axial level (cranial vs. vagal), so they descend from a common premigratory neural crest progenitor pool along a continuous rostrocaudal domain.

subtype:Cranial neural crest (anterior).name: Cranial neural crest (anterior)
subtype:Cranial neural crest (anterior).description: Cranial neural crest (anterior) cells are a subpopulation of cranial neural crest originating from the prosencephalic and mesencephalic neural folds that migrate into the frontonasal prominence and anterior pharyngeal arches. These cells give rise to much of the craniofacial mesenchyme—including cartilage, bone, and connective tissue of the face and anterior skull—and are captured here from E8.5 through E10.0 during active migration and early differentiation.

subtype:Cranial neural crest (posterior).name: Cranial neural crest (posterior)
subtype:Cranial neural crest (posterior).description: Cranial neural crest (posterior) cells are neural crest cells originating from the caudal cranial region, primarily the hindbrain (rhombomere) level. They migrate into the posterior pharyngeal arches and contribute to skeletal, connective tissue, and mesenchymal derivatives of the posterior head and neck. Present from E8.5 through E10.0, these cells span the period of active neural crest emigration, ventral migration, and colonization of pharyngeal arch targets.

type:Dorsal root ganglion neuron.name: Dorsal root ganglion neuron
type:Dorsal root ganglion neuron.description: Dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons are neural crest-derived sensory neurons that coalesce into ganglia flanking the spinal cord and relay somatosensory information—touch, pain, temperature, and proprioception—from the periphery to the central nervous system. Appearing from E9.0 onward, these cells represent newly differentiated sensory neurons emerging as trunk neural crest condenses into segmentally organized ganglia during mid-gestation mouse development.

topLinks.explanation: Dorsal root ganglion neurons differentiate directly from dorsal root ganglion progenitors (neural crest–derived sensory neuroblasts), so they share ancestry through an immediate precursor-to-product lineage relationship within the trunk neural crest.

Both derive from the common neural crest lineage delaminating from the dorsal neural tube—DRG sensory neurons from trunk-level crest and vagal neural crest from anterior somite levels—so they trace back to a shared premigratory neural crest progenitor pool.

Dorsal root ganglion sensory neurons are direct derivatives of trunk neural crest cells, which delaminate from the dorsal neural tube, migrate ventrally, and coalesce to form DRG, so the two share a common neural crest progenitor lineage.

Autonomic progenitors and dorsal root ganglion neurons both descend from trunk neural crest cells, which delaminate from the dorsal neural tube and generate both autonomic (sympathetic/parasympathetic) and sensory (DRG) lineages, so their linkage reflects a shared multipotent neural crest progenitor pool.

Both cell types derive from trunk neural crest cells, which delaminate from the dorsal neural tube and give rise to sensory neurons of the dorsal root ganglia as well as sympathetic/autonomic neurons of the peripheral nervous system.

type:Dorsal root ganglion progenitor.name: Dorsal root ganglion progenitor
type:Dorsal root ganglion progenitor.description: Dorsal root ganglion (DRG) progenitors are neural crest-derived precursor cells that give rise to the sensory neurons of the dorsal root ganglia, which flank the developing spinal cord. Present at E9.5–E10.0, these progenitors are actively proliferating and beginning to commit to a somatosensory neuron fate, ultimately producing the neurons responsible for relaying pain, touch, temperature, and proprioceptive information from the periphery to the central nervous system.

topLinks.explanation: Dorsal root ganglion progenitors are a direct derivative of trunk neural crest, which delaminates from the dorsal neural tube and migrates ventrally to form the sensory DRG neurons and glia, so the two cell types share a recent common neural-crest progenitor.

Dorsal root ganglion neurons differentiate directly from dorsal root ganglion progenitors (neural crest–derived sensory neuroblasts), so they share ancestry through an immediate precursor-to-product lineage relationship within the trunk neural crest.

Dorsal root ganglion progenitors and vagal neural crest both arise from the common premigratory neural crest lineage delaminating from the dorsal neural tube, with vagal (anterior) and trunk-level crest representing contiguous positions along the same axial progenitor pool.

Both autonomic (sympathetic/parasympathetic) and dorsal root ganglion sensory progenitors are derived from a common pool of trunk neural crest cells that delaminate from the dorsal neural tube and migrate ventrally, so their shared ancestry reflects this single multipotent neural crest origin.

Both derive from trunk neural crest cells, which delaminate from the dorsal neural tube and migrate to give rise to sensory neurons of the dorsal root ganglia and to autonomic (sympathetic/parasympathetic) neurons, so they share a common multipotent neural crest progenitor pool.

type:Frontonasal mesenchyme.name: Frontonasal mesenchyme
type:Frontonasal mesenchyme.description: Frontonasal mesenchyme is a neural crest-derived mesenchymal population that populates the frontonasal prominence of the developing embryo, ultimately contributing to midface structures including the nasal septum, nasal bridge, and forehead. This population emerges after cranial neural crest cells migrate into the frontonasal region and undergo an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, adopting a proliferative, matrix-producing mesenchymal identity that is patterned by retinoic acid and homeobox transcription factor gradients. Its presence from E8.5 through E10.0 is consistent with the progressive expansion of the frontonasal prominence during mid-gestation craniofacial morphogenesis.

topLinks.explanation: Both mesenchymal populations are predominantly derived from cranial neural crest cells emigrating from the dorsal midbrain/hindbrain neural folds, with frontonasal mesenchyme arising from forebrain–midbrain crest and pharyngeal arch mesenchyme from partially overlapping hindbrain crest streams, giving them a common ectomesenchymal progenitor origin.

Both derive from the anterior neural plate border / rostral head ectoderm, where cranial (frontonasal) neural-crest-derived mesenchyme and the preplacodal ectoderm that forms the olfactory placode arise as sister lineages and co-emerge within the developing frontonasal prominence.

Both trace to the anterior neural plate border ectoderm—frontonasal mesenchyme as forebrain/midbrain cranial neural crest ectomesenchyme and the trigeminal placode from the adjacent preplacodal ectoderm—so they arise as neighboring border derivatives that co-emerge in the same anterior head field (and even co-assemble the trigeminal ganglion).

Frontonasal mesenchyme is largely populated by cranial (frontonasal-prominence) neural crest cells that delaminate from the anterior neural folds and migrate ventrally, so both cell types descend from a shared cranial neural crest progenitor pool.

Frontonasal mesenchyme is cranial neural crest that delaminates from the anterior neural folds immediately adjacent to the prospective telencephalon, so both trace back to a shared anterior neuroectoderm/neural-plate-border progenitor pool in the forebrain region.

type:Pharyngeal arch mesenchyme.name: Pharyngeal arch mesenchyme
type:Pharyngeal arch mesenchyme.description: Pharyngeal arch mesenchyme comprises neural crest-derived mesenchymal cells that populate the pharyngeal (branchial) arches, transient embryonic structures that give rise to craniofacial skeletal elements, connective tissues, and smooth muscle of the face, jaw, and neck. These cells undergo extensive proliferation and patterning between E8.5 and E10.0 as the arches form and are colonized by migrating cranial neural crest, ultimately differentiating into chondrocytes, osteoblasts, and other connective tissue cell types of the head and pharyngeal region.

topLinks.explanation: Cranial neural crest cells delaminate from the dorsal neural folds and migrate ventrally into the pharyngeal arches where they form the ectomesenchyme, so pharyngeal arch mesenchyme is largely a direct descendant of cranial neural crest, giving them a shared progenitor origin.

Both cell types largely derive from cranial (mid-/hindbrain and first-arch) neural crest, which produces the ectomesenchyme filling the pharyngeal arches as well as the neural-crest-derived neurons of the trigeminal ganglion, so their shared ancestry reflects a common cranial neural crest progenitor pool.

Both mesenchymal populations are predominantly derived from cranial neural crest cells emigrating from the dorsal midbrain/hindbrain neural folds, with frontonasal mesenchyme arising from forebrain–midbrain crest and pharyngeal arch mesenchyme from partially overlapping hindbrain crest streams, giving them a common ectomesenchymal progenitor origin.

Pharyngeal arch mesenchyme is largely cranial neural-crest-derived ectomesenchyme, and neural crest delaminates from the dorsal neural tube at the neural plate border immediately adjacent to the roof plate, so both trace back to a common dorsal neuroectoderm / neural-plate-border progenitor pool.

Autonomic neuron progenitors and pharyngeal arch mesenchyme (ectomesenchyme) are both neural crest derivatives, sharing ancestry through a common cranial/cardiac-vagal neural crest progenitor pool that delaminates from the dorsal neural tube and migrates ventrally.

subtype:Pharyngeal arch mesenchyme (p1-p.name: Pharyngeal arch mesenchyme (p1-p2)
subtype:Pharyngeal arch mesenchyme (p1-p.description: Pharyngeal arch mesenchyme (p1-p2) comprises neural crest-derived mesenchymal cells that populate the first and second pharyngeal (branchial) arches during mid-gestation mouse development. These cells give rise to much of the craniofacial skeleton, including the jaw (mandible and maxilla from arch 1) and hyoid apparatus (from arch 2), as well as associated connective tissues, tendons, and smooth muscle. Their appearance from E8.5 through E10.0 is consistent with the timeline of cranial neural crest migration into the anterior arches.

subtype:Pharyngeal arch mesenchyme (p3-p.name: Pharyngeal arch mesenchyme (p3-p4)
subtype:Pharyngeal arch mesenchyme (p3-p.description: Pharyngeal arch mesenchyme (p3-p4) consists of neural crest-derived mesenchymal cells that populate the third and fourth pharyngeal arches during mid-embryogenesis. These arches give rise to skeletal and connective tissue elements of the lower jaw, hyoid, laryngeal cartilages, and associated vasculature including the great arteries. Appearing from E9.0 onward, this population is actively differentiating and being patterned by combinatorial Hox codes and retinoic acid signaling that distinguish it from more rostral arch mesenchyme.

type:Sacral neural crest.name: Sacral neural crest
type:Sacral neural crest.description: Sacral neural crest cells are a posterior neural crest population arising from the sacral (caudal) level of the neural tube during mid-to-late organogenesis. These cells undergo epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and migrate into surrounding tissues, where they contribute to the enteric nervous system of the hindgut, pelvic ganglia, and posterior mesenchymal derivatives. Their emergence at E9.0–E10.0 is consistent with the temporal window in which sacral-level neural crest delamination and migration occur in the mouse embryo.

topLinks.explanation: Sacral and trunk neural crest are both posterior neural crest subpopulations delaminating from the dorsal neural tube (neural-plate-border/roof-plate lineage) along the trunk-to-sacral axial continuum, largely fed by common posterior neuromesodermal-progenitor-derived neural tube, so they differ mainly in axial level rather than lineage of origin.

Sacral neural crest and lumbar spinal cord share ancestry because both are caudal derivatives of the same posterior neuroepithelium—the crest delaminating from the dorsal neural tube while the spinal cord forms its ventralized core—with their matched posterior (lumbosacral) identity seeded by common neuromesodermal progenitors (NMPs) in the tailbud/caudal lateral epiblast.

Both cell types derive from the posterior neural tube/neural plate border — sacral neural crest delaminates from the dorsal neural tube while thoracic spinal cord forms its ventral/intermediate compartment, and both are generated by the caudal neuromesodermal progenitor pool (tailbud/CLE) that builds the posterior neuraxis, so they share a common neuroectodermal progenitor.

Sacral neural crest and sacral spinal cord both arise from the same posterior/sacral neural tube neuroepithelium—neural crest delaminates from the dorsal neural tube at matched axial levels—likely tracing back to a shared caudal neural plate (and neuromesodermal progenitor–derived) progenitor pool.

Both are axial subpopulations of neural crest that delaminate from the dorsal neural tube of the caudal embryo and share the common neural-crest progenitor pool (and jointly seed the enteric nervous system), so their shared ancestry reflects a common posterior/trunk neural-crest origin.

type:Trigeminal ganglion neuron.name: Trigeminal ganglion neuron
type:Trigeminal ganglion neuron.description: Trigeminal ganglion neurons are sensory neurons of the trigeminal (cranial nerve V) ganglion, the largest cranial ganglion, which relays somatosensory information—including touch, pain, and temperature—from the face, oral cavity, and anterior cranium. Derived from both cranial neural crest and ectodermal placodes, these neurons begin differentiating and extending peripheral and central projections during E9.5–E10.0 in the mouse.

topLinks.explanation: Cranial (particularly the trigeminal-level) neural crest is the direct progenitor of the neurons of the trigeminal ganglion, so the two cell types share ancestry because the ganglion neurons delaminate and differentiate directly from cranial neural crest cells (with an additional contribution from trigeminal placodes).

Both cell types largely derive from cranial (mid-/hindbrain and first-arch) neural crest, which produces the ectomesenchyme filling the pharyngeal arches as well as the neural-crest-derived neurons of the trigeminal ganglion, so their shared ancestry reflects a common cranial neural crest progenitor pool.

Trigeminal ganglion neurons are directly generated by delamination and neurogenesis from the ophthalmic and maxillomandibular trigeminal placodes (a preplacodal-ectoderm derivative), making the placode a literal direct progenitor of these neurons and explaining their shared ancestry.

Both trace back to the dorsal neural tube/neural plate border: the roof plate is the dorsal-most neuroepithelium, and trigeminal ganglion neurons derive largely from cranial neural crest that delaminates from this same dorsal region, so they share a common dorsal neuroepithelial progenitor pool.

Both cell types derive from cranial (largely midbrain/hindbrain) neural crest — frontonasal mesenchyme is ectomesenchymal neural crest, and a substantial fraction of trigeminal ganglion neurons are neural-crest-derived — so they trace back to a shared premigratory cranial neural crest progenitor pool.

type:Trunk neural crest.name: Trunk neural crest
type:Trunk neural crest.description: Trunk neural crest cells are a migratory neural crest population originating from the post-otic axial levels of the closing neural tube, primarily giving rise to sensory and autonomic neurons of the peripheral nervous system, Schwann cell precursors, and melanocytes. Emerging from E8.5 onward in this dataset, they migrate along characteristic ventral and dorsolateral pathways adjacent to somites and are distinguished from cranial neural crest by their more posterior origin and restricted differentiation potential.

topLinks.explanation: Dorsal root ganglion progenitors are a direct derivative of trunk neural crest, which delaminates from the dorsal neural tube and migrates ventrally to form the sensory DRG neurons and glia, so the two cell types share a recent common neural-crest progenitor.

Both are neural crest populations delaminating from the dorsal neural tube along a continuous rostrocaudal axis, arising from a shared neural-plate-border/premigratory neural crest progenitor pool, with vagal crest occupying the posterior-hindbrain-to-anterior-trunk region that is spatially and developmentally contiguous with trunk crest.

Dorsal root ganglion sensory neurons are direct derivatives of trunk neural crest cells, which delaminate from the dorsal neural tube, migrate ventrally, and coalesce to form DRG, so the two share a common neural crest progenitor lineage.

Sacral and trunk neural crest are both posterior neural crest subpopulations delaminating from the dorsal neural tube (neural-plate-border/roof-plate lineage) along the trunk-to-sacral axial continuum, largely fed by common posterior neuromesodermal-progenitor-derived neural tube, so they differ mainly in axial level rather than lineage of origin.

Trunk neural crest cells migrating ventrally along the sympathoadrenal pathway are the direct progenitors of autonomic (sympathetic) neurons, so the two cell types are sequential stages of a single neural-crest-derived lineage sharing a common recent progenitor pool.

type:Vagal neural crest.name: Vagal neural crest
type:Vagal neural crest.description: Vagal neural crest cells are a migratory neural crest population originating from the post-otic hindbrain at somite levels 1–7. They give rise to the enteric nervous system of the gut, contribute to cardiac outflow tract septation, and populate pharyngeal arch–derived structures. These cells emerge during mid-somitogenesis and are essential for proper innervation and patterning of the developing gastrointestinal tract.

topLinks.explanation: Both are neural crest populations delaminating from the dorsal neural tube along a continuous rostrocaudal axis, arising from a shared neural-plate-border/premigratory neural crest progenitor pool, with vagal crest occupying the posterior-hindbrain-to-anterior-trunk region that is spatially and developmentally contiguous with trunk crest.

Autonomic progenitors are direct descendants of neural crest, and vagal (post-otic) neural crest is a well-established source of autonomic (parasympathetic/enteric and sympathoadrenal) neurons via a shared SOX10+/PHOX2B+ crest-derived progenitor pool, so the two cell types lie on the same delaminating-crest-to-autonomic-neuron lineage.

Dorsal root ganglion progenitors and vagal neural crest both arise from the common premigratory neural crest lineage delaminating from the dorsal neural tube, with vagal (anterior) and trunk-level crest representing contiguous positions along the same axial progenitor pool.

Both derive from the common neural crest lineage delaminating from the dorsal neural tube—DRG sensory neurons from trunk-level crest and vagal neural crest from anterior somite levels—so they trace back to a shared premigratory neural crest progenitor pool.

Autonomic neurons derive directly from neural crest, and vagal neural crest is the specific migratory progenitor population that seeds parasympathetic and enteric autonomic neurons, so they represent successive stages of one continuous lineage.

type:Amniotic ectoderm.name: Amniotic ectoderm
type:Amniotic ectoderm.description: Amniotic ectoderm is the inner ectodermal epithelial layer of the amnion, the thin membrane that encloses the embryo within the amniotic cavity. Continuous with but distinct from the embryonic ectoderm, it forms as the amniotic folds close around E7.5–E8.0 and persists as a simple squamous-to-cuboidal epithelium that provides a protective fluid-filled environment for the developing embryo. As an extraembryonic ectoderm derivative, it does not contribute to embryonic tissues but plays roles in signaling and mechanical protection.

topLinks.explanation: Both are non-neural squamous ectodermal epithelia derived from the pluripotent epiblast, with amniotic ectoderm arising from posterior/proximal epiblast adjacent to the primitive streak and surface (non-neural) ectoderm from embryonic ectoderm, so they share a recent common epiblast-derived progenitor pool.

Both amniotic ectoderm and epidermal progenitors derive from the same non-neural (surface) ectoderm lineage of the early epiblast, so they share a common Trp63+/Krt8+ surface-ectoderm progenitor pool rather than segregating into distinct germ-layer derivatives.

Both are epiblast-derived non-neural/surface ectoderm derivatives, so their shared ancestry likely reflects a common pool of early surface-ectoderm progenitors (the non-neural ectoderm domain from which the amnion and the neural-plate-border preplacodal ectoderm giving rise to epibranchial placodes both segregate).

Both derive from the early proximal/non-neural (surface) ectoderm of the epiblast—amniotic ectoderm buds off this pool during gastrulation while epibranchial sensory neurons arise from cranial (epibranchial placodal) ectoderm at the neural/non-neural border, so they likely share a common epiblast-derived non-neural ectoderm progenitor before amnion and placodal fates diverge.

Both derive from epiblast-descended non-neural (surface) ectoderm — the amniotic ectoderm and the pre-placodal cranial surface ectoderm that gives rise to the lens placode share a common Tfap2/Krt+ squamous ectodermal progenitor pool set aside early rather than committing to neural fate.

type:Extraembryonic ectoderm.name: Extraembryonic ectoderm
type:Extraembryonic ectoderm.description: Extraembryonic ectoderm is a transient trophoblast-derived epithelial tissue that forms the outer layer of the ectoplacental cone and lines the proamniotic cavity at pre- and early gastrulation stages. It contributes to the chorionic ectoderm and, ultimately, to the labyrinth layer of the placenta, playing essential roles in nutrient exchange, placental morphogenesis, and signaling to the underlying epiblast. Its restriction to E7.5 in this dataset is consistent with its rapid differentiation into downstream trophoblast subtypes during gastrulation.

type:Anterior mesoderm.name: Anterior mesoderm
type:Anterior mesoderm.description: Anterior mesoderm is a mesodermal population in the developing mouse embryo that gives rise to head mesenchyme, pharyngeal arch mesoderm, and portions of the second heart field. Present from E8.0 through E9.0, these cells contribute to craniofacial connective tissues, pharyngeal arch-derived structures, and outflow tract components of the developing heart.

type:Arterial endothelial cell.name: Arterial endothelial cell
type:Arterial endothelial cell.description: Arterial endothelial cells are vascular endothelial cells that line the inner walls of arteries, distinguished from venous and capillary endothelium by their unique molecular signature and role in maintaining high-pressure, oxygen-rich blood flow. In the mouse embryo from E8.5 onward, these cells emerge as the vascular plexus remodels into a hierarchical arterial-venous network, contributing to the dorsal aortae, pharyngeal arch arteries, and other major arterial vessels essential for embryonic circulation and organogenesis.

topLinks.explanation: Both arise from a shared hemangioblast/lateral-plate-mesoderm-derived endothelial progenitor pool, with hemogenic endothelium being an arterial-identity-specialized subset of the dorsal aorta/AGM endothelium (Notch/Runx1-driven) that undergoes endothelial-to-hematopoietic transition, so the two are essentially sibling states of the same arterial endothelial lineage.

Both likely descend from a common splanchnic/pharyngeal mesoderm progenitor pool, as second heart field (SHF) progenitors are multipotent and give rise not only to cardiomyocytes but also to endothelial/endocardial cells of the outflow tract and great arteries, explaining shared ancestry with arterial endothelial cells.

Arterial endothelial cells are a specialized subset of endothelial cells that differentiate (via VEGF/Notch signaling) from the same mesoderm-derived angioblast/hemangioblast progenitor pool that gives rise to the general endothelial population, so their shared ancestry reflects a direct subtype–parent lineage relationship.

Arterial endothelial cells arise from angioblasts/hemangioblast progenitors resident within the splanchnic (lateral plate) mesoderm, so both cell types descend from a common lateral-plate mesodermal progenitor pool.

Both cell types derive from the anterior splanchnic (cardiopharyngeal/second heart field) mesoderm, where bipotent angioblast-competent progenitors give rise to pharyngeal muscle mesenchyme as well as the arterial endothelium that lines the pharyngeal arch arteries and great vessels.

type:Endothelial cell.name: Endothelial cell
type:Endothelial cell.description: Endothelial cells form the inner lining of blood and lymphatic vessels throughout the embryo. Arising from lateral plate mesoderm, they are among the earliest vascular cell types to differentiate, establishing the primary vascular plexus during embryonic development and subsequently remodeling it into a mature circulatory network through vasculogenesis and angiogenesis.

topLinks.explanation: Both lineages are mesodermal derivatives arising from a shared lateral-plate/somatic mesoderm progenitor pool, from which FLK1+/KDR+ angioblasts delaminate out of the same mesenchyme that also forms the somatic (parietal) mesoderm.

Endothelial cells and splanchnic mesoderm share ancestry because both derive from lateral plate mesoderm, with the splanchnic (visceral) layer serving as a major source of hemangioblast/hemogenic-endothelial progenitors that generate the vascular endothelium of the gut, heart, and yolk sac.

Hemogenic endothelium is a specialized subset of vascular endothelium, and both arise from a common mesodermal endothelial/hemangioblast progenitor (lateral plate/extraembryonic mesoderm) before hemogenic endothelium diverges via the endothelial-to-hematopoietic transition, so they naturally share very recent common ancestors.

Both derive from Mesp1+ anterior splanchnic/cardiopharyngeal lateral-plate mesoderm, a multipotent progenitor field that co-generates pharyngeal (head/branchiomeric) muscle and mesodermal endothelial/endocardial cells.

Both cell types derive from lateral plate mesoderm—the forelimb field is somatopleuric LPM and much of the local limb/trunk vasculature arises from LPM-derived angioblasts (Flk1+/Etv2+ endothelial progenitors), so they emerge from a shared mesodermal progenitor pool.

type:Endothelial progenitor.name: Endothelial progenitor
type:Endothelial progenitor.description: Endothelial progenitors are mesodermal precursor cells that give rise to the vascular endothelium during embryonic vasculogenesis. Present from E8.0 onward, these cells are specified from lateral plate mesoderm and represent the earliest committed endothelial lineage, forming the primitive vascular plexus before maturing into the diverse endothelial subtypes that line blood and lymphatic vessels.

topLinks.explanation: Both cell types descend from the somitic dermomyotome, where Pax3+ progenitors are known to be bipotent for skeletal muscle and endothelium, so hypaxial (limb/body-wall) myogenic progenitors and endothelial progenitors co-emerge from this shared paraxial-mesoderm progenitor pool.

Both cell types descend from nascent posterior mesoderm ingressing through the primitive streak, and endothelial progenitors (angioblasts) are known to bud from the same intermediate/lateral mesodermal field that generates intermediate mesoderm, reflecting a shared FLK1+ mesodermal progenitor pool.

Both cell types arise from anterior/splanchnic (cardiopharyngeal-field) mesoderm, where a common Mesp1+ multipotent progenitor pool gives rise to pharyngeal/head mesoderm and to endothelial (endocardial/vascular) progenitors, explaining their recent shared ancestry.

Both cell types descend from paraxial (somitic) mesoderm, where the central dermomyotome acts as a demonstrated multipotent progenitor pool that generates not only dermis and myotome but also angioblasts/endothelial progenitors contributing to trunk and limb vasculature (dermomyotomal endothelial lineage, Ben-Yair & Kalcheim).

Both derive from paraxial (presomitic/somitic) mesoderm — sclerotome is the ventral somite compartment, and somite-derived angioblasts are a well-documented source of endothelial progenitors (contributing to the dorsal aorta and body-wall/limb vasculature), so the two share a common somitic progenitor pool.

type:Hematoendothelial progenitor.name: Hematoendothelial progenitor
type:Hematoendothelial progenitor.description: Hematoendothelial progenitors are bipotent mesodermal precursors that arise in the yolk sac blood islands during gastrulation and give rise to both primitive hematopoietic cells and vascular endothelium. Present at E7.5–E8.0, these cells represent the earliest branch point between blood and endothelial fates and are functionally related to the hemangioblast, a transient population specified from lateral and posterior mesoderm under the influence of BMP and Wnt signaling.

type:Hemogenic endothelium.name: Hemogenic endothelium
type:Hemogenic endothelium.description: Hemogenic endothelium is a specialized subset of vascular endothelial cells uniquely capable of undergoing endothelial-to-hematopoietic transition (EHT), giving rise to definitive hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells. Found primarily in the aorta-gonad-mesonephros (AGM) region, yolk sac, and placenta, these cells are present during a narrow developmental window (here E9.0–E10.0) that coincides with the onset of definitive hematopoiesis in the mouse embryo.

topLinks.explanation: Both cell types derive from the same early lateral plate/posterior mesoderm progenitor pool, with hemogenic endothelium (the source of definitive blood via endothelial-to-hematopoietic transition) and somatic (somatopleuric) mesoderm splitting from a common Mesp1+ nascent mesodermal lineage during gastrulation.

Hemogenic endothelium arises from the same lateral plate/splanchnic mesoderm progenitor pool that generates yolk-sac and gut-associated endothelium and blood islands, so both cell types descend from a shared posterior/visceral lateral plate mesoderm lineage (via hemangioblast/hemogenic endothelial specification).

Both arise from a shared hemangioblast/lateral-plate-mesoderm-derived endothelial progenitor pool, with hemogenic endothelium being an arterial-identity-specialized subset of the dorsal aorta/AGM endothelium (Notch/Runx1-driven) that undergoes endothelial-to-hematopoietic transition, so the two are essentially sibling states of the same arterial endothelial lineage.

Hemogenic endothelium is a specialized subset of vascular endothelium, and both arise from a common mesodermal endothelial/hemangioblast progenitor (lateral plate/extraembryonic mesoderm) before hemogenic endothelium diverges via the endothelial-to-hematopoietic transition, so they naturally share very recent common ancestors.

Both derive from posterior lateral plate/nascent mesoderm ingressing through the caudal primitive streak, where hindlimb-field mesenchyme and Kdr+ hemogenic-endothelial (hemangioblast-like) progenitors co-emerge from a shared posterior mesodermal progenitor pool.

type:Nascent mesoderm.name: Nascent mesoderm
type:Nascent mesoderm.description: Nascent mesoderm comprises the earliest mesodermal progenitors that have just delaminated from the primitive streak during gastrulation, having undergone epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition but not yet diversified into specific mesodermal subtypes. Present at E7.5–E8.0, these cells represent a transient state bridging epiblast exit and mesodermal lineage commitment, retaining residual pluripotency features while activating the core mesoderm transcriptional program.

type:Notochord.name: Notochord
type:Notochord.description: The notochord is a rod-shaped mesodermal structure running along the embryonic dorsal midline that serves as the primary axial scaffold and a critical ventral midline signaling center. It secretes morphogens that pattern the neural tube and somites, and in later development its remnants contribute to the nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral discs. Present from E7.5 through E10.0 in this dataset, the notochord is one of the earliest and most persistent mesodermal derivatives of the organizer.

topLinks.explanation: Both cell types likely descend from the anterior primitive streak/node (axial mesendoderm), the region that ingresses to form definitive foregut endoderm (giving rise to hepatoblasts) and the notochordal plate, which transiently intercalates into the gut endoderm before segregating as notochord.

Both the notochord (axial mesoderm) and pharyngeal/foregut endoderm arise from the node and anterior primitive streak during gastrulation, sharing an axial mesendoderm progenitor pool in which notochordal-plate cells transiently intercalate with the definitive endoderm before segregating.

Both arise from the Foxa2+ anterior primitive streak/node-derived axial mesendoderm, where early notochord progenitors are transiently intercalated within the definitive (gut) endoderm before delaminating, giving foregut and notochord a shared progenitor pool.

Both the notochord and the medial floor plate descend from Foxa2/Shh-expressing axial progenitors in the node/organizer (axial mesendoderm), so their shared ancestry reflects a common node-derived lineage rather than only the classic notochord-to-floor-plate Shh induction.

Both cell types emerge from the anterior primitive streak/node region during gastrulation, where axial (notochord) progenitors and cranial paraxial mesoderm progenitors are closely juxtaposed and share a common node-derived mesodermal progenitor pool.

type:Prechordal plate.name: Prechordal plate
type:Prechordal plate.description: The prechordal plate is a specialized axial mesendodermal structure situated at the anterior tip of the notochord, directly beneath the developing forebrain. It functions as a critical ventral midline signaling center during early embryogenesis, secreting morphogens that pattern the ventral forebrain, induce the hypothalamus, and establish bilateral symmetry of craniofacial structures. Its presence from E7.5 through E9.0 is consistent with its role in head organizer activity during gastrulation and early organogenesis.

type:Endocardial cell.name: Endocardial cell
type:Endocardial cell.description: Endocardial cells are the specialized endothelial cells that line the inner surface of the developing heart chambers. Arising from lateral plate mesoderm, they play essential roles in cardiac morphogenesis including valve formation, trabeculation, and endocardial-to-mesenchymal transition (EndMT) that contributes to the cardiac cushions and septa. Their appearance from E8.5 onward is consistent with the timing of heart tube formation and subsequent chamber remodeling in the mouse embryo.

topLinks.explanation: Endocardial cells and first-heart-field myocardium both descend from Mesp1+/Nkx2-5+ multipotent cardiovascular progenitors in the cardiac crescent, which are known to be bipotent for endocardial and myocardial fates.

Both cell types derive from the Mesp1+ anterior/cardiogenic splanchnic mesoderm, with endocardial (endothelial) cells and second-heart-field myocardial progenitors emerging from a shared multipotent cardiovascular progenitor pool (Isl1+/Nkx2-5+) that lineage-tracing has shown gives rise to both endocardium and SHF derivatives.

Endocardial cells and epicardium both derive from cardiogenic lateral plate mesoderm (juxta-cardiac field/proepicardial region), where a common Nkx2.5/Isl1-lineage cardiac mesodermal progenitor pool gives rise to both the endothelial lining and the epicardial covering of the developing heart, explaining their shared recent ancestry.

Both cell types descend from Mesp1+ anterior lateral-plate (cardiogenic) mesoderm of the cardiac crescent, where the juxtacardiac field is a recently described multipotent progenitor pool that co-emerges with, and shares clones with, the endocardial/endothelial precursors lining the forming heart.

Both derive from the anterior splanchnic/lateral plate mesoderm of the cardiopharyngeal field (Mesp1+ second-heart-field progenitors), where endocardial endothelium and pharyngeal/branchiomeric mesoderm co-emerge from a shared multipotent progenitor pool.

type:Epicardium.name: Epicardium
type:Epicardium.description: The epicardium is the outermost mesothelial layer enveloping the developing heart, derived from the proepicardial organ of the lateral plate mesoderm. Emerging around E9.0 as proepicardial cells migrate onto and spread across the myocardial surface, the epicardium serves as a critical signaling center for myocardial growth and as a source of progenitors that undergo epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition to generate cardiac fibroblasts, coronary vascular smooth muscle cells, and pericytes.

topLinks.explanation: Both the epicardium (via the proepicardium) and the second heart field derive from a shared pool of cardiogenic lateral plate/splanchnic mesoderm—the juxta-cardiac field/posterior second heart field—whose progenitors give rise to both the epicardial lineage and SHF-derived myocardium.

The juxtacardiac field—a Mab21l2+/Hand1+ pool of anterior lateral plate mesoderm adjacent to the cardiac crescent—is a recently defined progenitor source that directly gives rise to the epicardium (and septum transversum), so the two cell types descend from this shared JCF/lateral plate mesoderm progenitor.

Both derive from the same anterior lateral-plate/cardiogenic mesoderm—specifically the first heart field and its adjacent juxta-cardiac field, a bipotent pool that gives rise to both myocardium and the proepicardium/epicardium.

Endocardial cells and epicardium both derive from cardiogenic lateral plate mesoderm (juxta-cardiac field/proepicardial region), where a common Nkx2.5/Isl1-lineage cardiac mesodermal progenitor pool gives rise to both the endothelial lining and the epicardial covering of the developing heart, explaining their shared recent ancestry.

Both epicardium (via the proepicardium/juxta-cardiac field) and pharyngeal mesoderm (second heart field and head-muscle progenitors) arise from the anterior lateral plate mesoderm / cardiopharyngeal field, so they share recent common progenitors in this cardiogenic-splanchnic domain.

type:First heart field.name: First heart field
type:First heart field.description: The first heart field (FHF) is a population of cardiac progenitor cells derived from lateral plate mesoderm that gives rise to the left ventricle and parts of the atria of the developing heart. FHF cells are among the earliest specified cardiac progenitors, differentiating into cardiomyocytes beginning around E8.0 as the linear heart tube forms, and they represent the primary contractile cells of the early embryonic heart.

topLinks.explanation: Both derive from the same anterior lateral-plate/cardiogenic mesoderm—specifically the first heart field and its adjacent juxta-cardiac field, a bipotent pool that gives rise to both myocardium and the proepicardium/epicardium.

Endocardial cells and first-heart-field myocardium both descend from Mesp1+/Nkx2-5+ multipotent cardiovascular progenitors in the cardiac crescent, which are known to be bipotent for endocardial and myocardial fates.

Both fields arise from the same Mesp1+ anterior cardiogenic (splanchnic) mesoderm, with the juxta-cardiac field described as a common progenitor pool that directly feeds first-heart-field cardiomyocytes (and epicardium), so their strong shared ancestry reflects a recent common cardiac-mesoderm progenitor.

The first and second heart fields both derive from the common cardiogenic (anterior splanchnic) mesoderm arising from the early cardiac crescent, so they share a recent Mesp1+ cardiac progenitor pool.

Both cell types likely descend from the early anterior mesoderm that ingresses through the anterior primitive streak during gastrulation—the first heart field arising from anterior splanchnic lateral plate/cardiac crescent mesoderm and the mesodermal component of the periocular mesenchyme from adjacent cranial/paraxial (head) mesoderm—so they share a common anterior mesodermal progenitor pool before splitting into cardiac versus cranial fates.

subtype:Atrioventricular canal.name: Atrioventricular canal
subtype:Atrioventricular canal.description: The atrioventricular canal (AVC) is a specialized myocardial region of the first heart field that forms the constriction between the developing atrial and ventricular chambers during mid-gestation. It serves as the precursor to the atrioventricular valves and septum, and its myocardium orchestrates endocardial-to-mesenchymal transition in the adjacent cardiac cushions. Present from E8.5 through E10.0, these cells are central to cardiac septation and valve morphogenesis.

subtype:Left ventricle.name: Left ventricle
subtype:Left ventricle.description: Left ventricular cardiomyocytes are the contractile muscle cells of the left ventricle, the principal systemic pumping chamber of the heart. Derived from the first heart field, these cells are among the earliest specified cardiac lineages in the mouse embryo, emerging around E8.0–E8.5 as the linear heart tube loops and chambers begin to form. By E9.5–E10.0, left ventricular cardiomyocytes are actively proliferating and establishing the compact and trabecular myocardial layers that will support systemic circulation.

type:Forelimb field.name: Forelimb field
type:Forelimb field.description: The forelimb field comprises lateral plate mesoderm progenitors at the forelimb level that condense and proliferate to initiate the forelimb bud between E9.5 and E10.0. These cells give rise to the skeletal, connective tissue, and tendon elements of the forelimb, and are distinguished from hindlimb progenitors by a distinct transcription factor code.

topLinks.explanation: The forelimb field and mesothelium share ancestry because both arise from the somatic layer of the lateral plate mesoderm (somatopleure)—the forelimb bud from the somatopleuric LPM and the coelomic mesothelium from the same LPM sheet lining the body cavity.

The forelimb field is a regional subdomain of the somatic (parietal) layer of the lateral plate mesoderm, so both cell types derive from the same somatic lateral plate mesoderm progenitor pool that forms the limb bud mesenchyme and body wall.

Both cell types descend from lateral plate mesoderm, which splits into a somatic (parietal) layer giving rise to the limb-field mesenchyme and a splanchnic (visceral) layer, so their shared ancestry reflects a common lateral-plate mesoderm progenitor pool prior to the somatic/splanchnic bifurcation.

Both cell types derive from lateral plate mesoderm—the forelimb field is somatopleuric LPM and much of the local limb/trunk vasculature arises from LPM-derived angioblasts (Flk1+/Etv2+ endothelial progenitors), so they emerge from a shared mesodermal progenitor pool.

Both arise from mesoderm at the same forelimb axial level—the forelimb field being lateral plate mesoderm and hypaxial myogenic progenitors delaminating from the adjacent limb-level dermomyotome (paraxial mesoderm)—so they trace back to a shared posterior/paraxial-plus-lateral mesodermal progenitor pool at that axial position, consistent with the muscle progenitors' migration into and co-emergence with the limb field.

type:Hindlimb field.name: Hindlimb field
type:Hindlimb field.description: The hindlimb field comprises lateral plate mesoderm progenitors that coalesce at the posterior flank of the embryo to form the hindlimb bud, emerging around E9.5 — slightly later than the forelimb field. These cells give rise to the skeletal, connective tissue, and dermal components of the hindlimb, and are specified by a unique combination of transcription factors that distinguish them from forelimb and other lateral plate mesoderm populations.

topLinks.explanation: The hindlimb field is a direct derivative of the somatic (parietal) layer of the lateral plate mesoderm, so both cell types descend from a shared somatopleuric lateral-plate mesoderm progenitor pool.

The hindlimb field (posterior lateral plate mesoderm) and intermediate mesoderm both ingress from the posterior primitive streak at overlapping caudal axial levels and remain spatially adjacent, so they share a common posterior/caudal mesodermal progenitor pool before the LPM–IM split is resolved.

Both cell types derive from the lateral plate mesoderm, which splits into a somatic (parietal) layer giving rise to the hindlimb field and a splanchnic (visceral) layer, so they share a recent common LPM progenitor pool—likely the posterior lateral plate mesoderm.
Both arise from posterior primitive-streak-derived caudal mesoderm — the Tbx4/Isl1-expressing posterior lateral-plate/extraembryonic mesoderm pool that produces the allantois and the hindlimb field.

The epidermal progenitors overlying the posterior body wall and the hindlimb-field lateral plate mesoderm likely co-emerge from the same caudal epiblast/primitive-streak territory, so a shared regional posterior-epiblast progenitor pool couples surface ectoderm and limb-field mesoderm despite their different germ layers.

type:Juxtacardiac field.name: Juxtacardiac field
type:Juxtacardiac field.description: The juxtacardiac field (JCF) is a lateral plate mesoderm-derived progenitor population situated adjacent to the cardiac crescent and developing heart tube. These cells contribute to the pericardium, ventral body wall mesenchyme, and portions of the heart, serving as a transitional progenitor pool that bridges cardiac and somatic lateral plate fates. Present from E8.0 through E10.0, the JCF persists as a mesenchymal population flanking the heart during organogenesis.

topLinks.explanation: Both fields derive from the anterior/cardiogenic lateral plate mesoderm (splanchnic/cardiopharyngeal mesoderm) flanking the cardiac crescent, so the juxtacardiac field and second heart field descend from a shared pool of cardiogenic lateral plate mesoderm progenitors.

The juxtacardiac field—a Mab21l2+/Hand1+ pool of anterior lateral plate mesoderm adjacent to the cardiac crescent—is a recently defined progenitor source that directly gives rise to the epicardium (and septum transversum), so the two cell types descend from this shared JCF/lateral plate mesoderm progenitor.

Both cell types descend from the anterior lateral plate mesoderm—specifically the cardiopharyngeal mesoderm field where the juxtacardiac field lies contiguous with the cardiac crescent and pharyngeal (second-heart-field) mesoderm, so they share Mesp1+ anterior splanchnic mesoderm progenitors.

Both fields arise from the same Mesp1+ anterior cardiogenic (splanchnic) mesoderm, with the juxta-cardiac field described as a common progenitor pool that directly feeds first-heart-field cardiomyocytes (and epicardium), so their strong shared ancestry reflects a recent common cardiac-mesoderm progenitor.

Both cell types descend from Mesp1+ anterior lateral-plate (cardiogenic) mesoderm of the cardiac crescent, where the juxtacardiac field is a recently described multipotent progenitor pool that co-emerges with, and shares clones with, the endocardial/endothelial precursors lining the forming heart.

type:Lateral plate mesoderm.name: Lateral plate mesoderm
type:Lateral plate mesoderm.description: Lateral plate mesoderm (LPM) is a broad sheet of mesoderm that forms lateral to the paraxial and intermediate mesoderm during early gastrulation and body plan establishment. Present at E7.5–E8.0, this population represents the early, largely undifferentiated LPM prior to its splitting into somatic (body wall, limb) and splanchnic (heart, gut, vascular smooth muscle) layers, and serves as a common progenitor for diverse mesodermal derivatives including cardiovascular, hematopoietic, and visceral mesenchymal lineages.

type:Mesothelium.name: Mesothelium
type:Mesothelium.description: Mesothelium is the specialized simple squamous epithelium derived from lateral plate mesoderm that lines the coelomic cavities (pericardial, pleural, and peritoneal). Emerging at E9.5 as the intraembryonic coelom cavitates, mesothelial cells serve as a signaling center that produces retinoic acid to pattern adjacent developing organs, and later contribute progenitors to the vasculature and connective tissue of visceral organs through epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition.

topLinks.explanation: The forelimb field and mesothelium share ancestry because both arise from the somatic layer of the lateral plate mesoderm (somatopleure)—the forelimb bud from the somatopleuric LPM and the coelomic mesothelium from the same LPM sheet lining the body cavity.

Visceral (serosal) mesothelium is a direct derivative of the splanchnic layer of lateral plate mesoderm, which delaminates to line the coelomic cavity and coat the gut and visceral organs, so both cell types descend from the same splanchnic lateral plate mesodermal progenitor pool.

Mesothelium lining the body wall and coelomic cavities differentiates directly from the somatopleuric (somatic) layer of the lateral plate mesoderm, so the two cell types share a recent common lateral-plate-mesoderm progenitor pool.

Both cell types are mesodermal derivatives whose progenitors emerge adjacently from the posterior primitive streak/tailbud mesoderm and co-develop in the ventrolateral body wall—where somite-derived (dermomyotomal) hypaxial muscle precursors migrate into somatopleuric lateral-plate mesoderm that forms coelomic mesothelium—reflecting a shared common mesodermal progenitor pool rather than a single defined bipotent cell.

Endothelial cells and mesothelium both arise from lateral plate mesoderm—likely a shared splanchnic/hemato-vascular mesodermal progenitor pool—and mesothelium (e.g., epicardium/serosa) is itself a known source of endothelium via EMT during early organogenesis.

type:Second heart field.name: Second heart field
type:Second heart field.description: The second heart field (SHF) is a population of cardiac progenitor cells located in the pharyngeal and splanchnic mesoderm that progressively contributes to the elongating heart tube. SHF progenitors give rise to the outflow tract, right ventricle, and portions of the atria, complementing the first heart field which primarily forms the left ventricle. Its presence from E8.0 through E10.0 aligns with the period of active heart tube elongation, looping, and chamber septation in the mouse embryo.

topLinks.explanation: Both fields derive from the anterior/cardiogenic lateral plate mesoderm (splanchnic/cardiopharyngeal mesoderm) flanking the cardiac crescent, so the juxtacardiac field and second heart field descend from a shared pool of cardiogenic lateral plate mesoderm progenitors.

Both the epicardium (via the proepicardium) and the second heart field derive from a shared pool of cardiogenic lateral plate/splanchnic mesoderm—the juxta-cardiac field/posterior second heart field—whose progenitors give rise to both the epicardial lineage and SHF-derived myocardium.

The second heart field is a sub-population of the anterior pharyngeal (splanchnic) mesoderm, both deriving from the common cardiopharyngeal mesoderm progenitor pool (Mesp1+ anterior mesoderm) that co-generates outflow-tract cardiomyocytes and branchiomeric/pharyngeal muscle, so their shared ancestry reflects direct lineage continuity rather than mere co-emergence.

Both cell types derive from the Mesp1+ anterior/cardiogenic splanchnic mesoderm, with endocardial (endothelial) cells and second-heart-field myocardial progenitors emerging from a shared multipotent cardiovascular progenitor pool (Isl1+/Nkx2-5+) that lineage-tracing has shown gives rise to both endocardium and SHF derivatives.

The second heart field is a subpopulation of anterior splanchnic (lateral plate) mesoderm, so both derive from the same splanchnic mesodermal progenitor pool in the pharyngeal/cardiac crescent region and share near-immediate common ancestry.

subtype:Atria.name: Atria
subtype:Atria.description: Atrial cardiomyocytes are the contractile muscle cells that form the atrial chambers of the developing heart. Derived from second heart field progenitors, these cells differentiate during mid-embryogenesis (E8.5–E10.0) and acquire distinct electrophysiological and contractile properties that distinguish them from ventricular cardiomyocytes. They play essential roles in receiving blood flow and coordinating cardiac rhythm in the forming four-chambered heart.

subtype:Inflow tract.name: Inflow tract
subtype:Inflow tract.description: The inflow tract (venous pole) is the caudal segment of the embryonic heart tube that receives systemic venous return and gives rise to the sinus venosus, sinoatrial node, and atrial chambers. Derived from the posterior second heart field, these cardiomyocytes are actively differentiating during E9.0–E10.0 as the heart tube undergoes looping and chamber septation. This population is critical for establishing the cardiac pacemaker and patterning the atrial myocardium.

subtype:Outflow tract.name: Outflow tract
subtype:Outflow tract.description: The outflow tract is a transient embryonic cardiac structure derived from the second heart field that connects the developing ventricles to the pharyngeal arch arteries. During E9.0–E10.0, it undergoes elongation, looping, and eventual septation to form the proximal segments of the aorta and pulmonary trunk. It comprises myocardial, smooth muscle, and mesenchymal cell populations and is a major site of congenital heart defects when its development is perturbed.

subtype:Right ventricle.name: Right ventricle
subtype:Right ventricle.description: The right ventricle is a muscular chamber of the developing heart responsible for pumping blood into the pulmonary circulation. In the mouse embryo, it is primarily derived from the second heart field and becomes morphologically distinct as cardiac looping and septation progress between E8.5 and E10.0. Right ventricular cardiomyocytes undergo rapid proliferation and maturation during this window, establishing the compact and trabecular myocardial layers that will support postnatal cardiac function.

subtype:Second heart field (anterior).name: Second heart field (anterior)
subtype:Second heart field (anterior).description: The anterior second heart field is a population of cardiac progenitor cells derived from the pharyngeal mesoderm that contributes primarily to the outflow tract, right ventricle, and portions of the interventricular septum during heart development. Present from E8.0 through E10.0, these progenitors progressively differentiate into cardiomyocytes as they are deployed to the arterial pole of the elongating heart tube.

subtype:Second heart field (posterior).name: Second heart field (posterior)
subtype:Second heart field (posterior).description: The posterior second heart field (pSHF) is a subdomain of cardiac mesoderm progenitors that contributes primarily to the atria, sinus venosus, and dorsal mesenchymal protrusion of the developing heart. These progenitors are distinguished from their anterior counterparts by distinct signaling environments and transcription factor expression, and they play a critical role in atrial septation and pulmonary vein development during mid-gestational cardiogenesis.

type:Somatic mesoderm.name: Somatic mesoderm
type:Somatic mesoderm.description: Somatic mesoderm is the layer of lateral plate mesoderm that lies adjacent to the surface ectoderm, forming the somatopleure. It gives rise to the body wall musculature, connective tissues, limb bud mesenchyme, and the parietal lining of the coelomic cavities. Present from E8.5 onward, this large population expands as the embryo grows and the body wall and limbs elaborate.

topLinks.explanation: The hindlimb field is a direct derivative of the somatic (parietal) layer of the lateral plate mesoderm, so both cell types descend from a shared somatopleuric lateral-plate mesoderm progenitor pool.

Somatic (parietal) and splanchnic (visceral) mesoderm are the two layers formed when the lateral plate mesoderm splits at the coelomic cavity, so they share a common lateral plate mesoderm progenitor pool.

The forelimb field is a regional subdomain of the somatic (parietal) layer of the lateral plate mesoderm, so both cell types derive from the same somatic lateral plate mesoderm progenitor pool that forms the limb bud mesenchyme and body wall.

Both cell types are derivatives of a common posterior/mid primitive-streak-derived nascent mesoderm progenitor pool that patterns along the mediolateral axis, with intermediate mesoderm and the somatic (parietal) layer of lateral plate mesoderm emerging as adjacent, closely related fates from this same lateral-mesodermal lineage.

Both arise from posterior primitive-streak/nascent mesoderm, with the allantois forming as an extraembryonic extension of the same lateral-plate (somatopleuric) mesoderm program that produces somatic mesoderm, giving them a shared posterior-mesodermal progenitor origin.

subtype:Somatic mesoderm (anterior).name: Somatic mesoderm (anterior)
subtype:Somatic mesoderm (anterior).description: Somatic mesoderm (anterior) is the dorsal layer of the lateral plate mesoderm positioned in the anterior (rostral) body axis of the mouse embryo. It forms the somatopleure together with overlying ectoderm and gives rise to anterior body wall connective tissue, limb bud mesenchyme, and dermis. This population expands from E8.5 onward as the lateral plate splits and the embryo undergoes anterior morphogenesis.

subtype:Somatic mesoderm (posterior).name: Somatic mesoderm (posterior)
subtype:Somatic mesoderm (posterior).description: Somatic mesoderm (posterior) is the caudal portion of the somatic (parietal) layer of the lateral plate mesoderm, which lines the body wall and contributes to the limb bud mesenchyme of the developing hindlimb. Present from E9.0 to E10.0, this population gives rise to connective tissue, skeletal elements, and dermis of the posterior trunk and hindlimb, and is distinguished from its anterior counterpart by a distinct positional identity along the anteroposterior axis.

subtype:Somatic mesoderm (tailbud).name: Somatic mesoderm (tailbud)
subtype:Somatic mesoderm (tailbud).description: Somatic mesoderm (tailbud) is a population of lateral plate mesoderm-derived cells localized to the posterior tailbud region of the mouse embryo during mid-gestation (E9.0–E10.0). The somatic (parietal) layer of lateral plate mesoderm gives rise to body wall mesenchyme, limb bud mesenchyme, and connective tissues, and this subtype specifically represents the caudal extension of that lineage as the embryo elongates through the tailbud. These cells contribute to the mesenchymal framework of the posterior trunk and tail.

type:Splanchnic mesoderm.name: Splanchnic mesoderm
type:Splanchnic mesoderm.description: Splanchnic mesoderm is the visceral (medial) layer of the lateral plate mesoderm that closely apposes the endoderm-derived gut tube. It gives rise to the mesenchyme of the visceral organs, including the smooth muscle and connective tissue of the gastrointestinal and respiratory tracts, the heart, and the spleen, and it plays a critical role in reciprocal signaling with the adjacent endoderm to pattern these organ primordia.

topLinks.explanation: Somatic (parietal) and splanchnic (visceral) mesoderm are the two layers formed when the lateral plate mesoderm splits at the coelomic cavity, so they share a common lateral plate mesoderm progenitor pool.

Both cell types descend from lateral plate mesoderm, which splits into a somatic (parietal) layer giving rise to the limb-field mesenchyme and a splanchnic (visceral) layer, so their shared ancestry reflects a common lateral-plate mesoderm progenitor pool prior to the somatic/splanchnic bifurcation.

Both cell types derive from the lateral plate mesoderm, which splits into a somatic (parietal) layer giving rise to the hindlimb field and a splanchnic (visceral) layer, so they share a recent common LPM progenitor pool—likely the posterior lateral plate mesoderm.

The second heart field is a subpopulation of anterior splanchnic (lateral plate) mesoderm, so both derive from the same splanchnic mesodermal progenitor pool in the pharyngeal/cardiac crescent region and share near-immediate common ancestry.

Visceral (serosal) mesothelium is a direct derivative of the splanchnic layer of lateral plate mesoderm, which delaminates to line the coelomic cavity and coat the gut and visceral organs, so both cell types descend from the same splanchnic lateral plate mesodermal progenitor pool.

subtype:Splanchnic mesoderm (cardiopulmo.name: Splanchnic mesoderm (cardiopulmonary)
subtype:Splanchnic mesoderm (cardiopulmo.description: Splanchnic mesoderm (cardiopulmonary) is a population of visceral lateral plate mesoderm that gives rise to the heart and the mesenchymal components of the developing lung. Appearing from E8.5 onward, these cells encompass the second heart field progenitors and the pulmonary mesoderm that surrounds the nascent lung buds, contributing to cardiomyocytes, cardiac outflow tract, and pulmonary smooth muscle and vasculature. This population bridges cardiac and respiratory mesoderm fates, which share a common origin in the anterior and posterior splanchnic mesoderm.

subtype:Splanchnic mesoderm (gastric).name: Splanchnic mesoderm (gastric)
subtype:Splanchnic mesoderm (gastric).description: Splanchnic mesoderm (gastric) is the visceral mesenchyme enveloping the developing stomach, derived from the splanchnic layer of lateral plate mesoderm that lines the foregut endoderm. Present at E9.5–E10.0, these cells provide inductive signals that pattern the gastric epithelium and ultimately give rise to the smooth muscle, connective tissue, and submucosal layers of the stomach wall.

subtype:Splanchnic mesoderm (intestinal).name: Splanchnic mesoderm (intestinal)
subtype:Splanchnic mesoderm (intestinal).description: Splanchnic mesoderm (intestinal) is the visceral layer of lateral plate mesoderm that ensheathes the developing midgut and hindgut endoderm, giving rise to the smooth muscle, connective tissue, and vasculature of the intestinal wall. Present from E8.5 through E10.0, this population expands as the gut tube elongates and begins regional patterning along the anterior-posterior axis. It serves as a critical signaling center that directs intestinal epithelial morphogenesis through reciprocal mesenchymal-epithelial interactions.

subtype:Splanchnic mesoderm (septum tran.name: Splanchnic mesoderm (septum transversum)
subtype:Splanchnic mesoderm (septum tran.description: The septum transversum is a mesodermal partition that forms between the developing heart and the foregut endoderm during mid-gestation, serving as a critical signaling center for hepatic induction and contributing to the diaphragm, epicardium, and hepatic stellate cells. This splanchnic mesoderm subpopulation appears from E8.5 onward as the septum transversum condenses ventral to the heart, producing mesenchymal cells that secrete signals (including BMPs and FGFs) essential for directing foregut endoderm toward a liver fate. It also gives rise to the proepicardial organ and stellate cell precursors that later colonize the liver bud.

type:Intermediate mesoderm.name: Intermediate mesoderm
type:Intermediate mesoderm.description: Intermediate mesoderm (IM) is a strip of mesoderm situated between the paraxial and lateral plate mesoderm along the anteroposterior axis of the embryo. It gives rise to the urogenital system, including the pronephros, mesonephros, and metanephros (definitive kidney), as well as the gonads and associated ductal structures. IM specification begins around E8.0 and proceeds in an anterior-to-posterior wave, consistent with this cluster's presence from E8.0 through E10.0.

topLinks.explanation: The hindlimb field (posterior lateral plate mesoderm) and intermediate mesoderm both ingress from the posterior primitive streak at overlapping caudal axial levels and remain spatially adjacent, so they share a common posterior/caudal mesodermal progenitor pool before the LPM–IM split is resolved.

Both cell types are derivatives of a common posterior/mid primitive-streak-derived nascent mesoderm progenitor pool that patterns along the mediolateral axis, with intermediate mesoderm and the somatic (parietal) layer of lateral plate mesoderm emerging as adjacent, closely related fates from this same lateral-mesodermal lineage.

Both derive from adjacent mediolateral domains of nascent trunk mesoderm ingressing through the anterior/mid primitive streak (fed by the caudal NMP/posterior progenitor pool), so the dermomyotome (dorsal paraxial/somite derivative) and the immediately lateral intermediate mesoderm share recently divergent mesodermal progenitors.

Both cell types descend from nascent posterior mesoderm ingressing through the primitive streak, and endothelial progenitors (angioblasts) are known to bud from the same intermediate/lateral mesodermal field that generates intermediate mesoderm, reflecting a shared FLK1+ mesodermal progenitor pool.

Both are adjacent mediolateral derivatives of nascent trunk mesoderm ingressing through the posterior primitive streak, so intermediate mesoderm and splanchnic (lateral plate) mesoderm descend from a shared, spatially contiguous lateral mesodermal progenitor pool before their mediolateral fates are fixed.

subtype:Intermediate mesoderm (nephrogen.name: Intermediate mesoderm (nephrogenic)
subtype:Intermediate mesoderm (nephrogen.description: Intermediate mesoderm (nephrogenic) represents the subset of intermediate mesoderm that has become specified toward the kidney-forming (nephrogenic) lineage during mid-gestation mouse development (E9.0–E10.0). These cells give rise to the nephric duct (Wolffian duct), mesonephric tubules, and ultimately contribute progenitors to the metanephric kidney, constituting the earliest committed renal precursor population in the embryo.

subtype:Intermediate mesoderm (posterior.name: Intermediate mesoderm (posterior)
subtype:Intermediate mesoderm (posterior.description: Intermediate mesoderm (posterior) represents the caudal segment of the intermediate mesoderm, the mesodermal territory positioned between the paraxial and lateral plate mesoderm that gives rise to the urogenital system. At E9.5–E10.0, this posterior population corresponds to less differentiated IM progenitors that will form the mesonephric and metanephric (definitive kidney) primordia, in contrast to more anterior IM that has already initiated nephric duct and tubule morphogenesis.

type:Dermomyotome.name: Dermomyotome
type:Dermomyotome.description: The dermomyotome is the dorsal epithelial layer of the maturing somite that serves as a multipotent progenitor pool for skeletal muscle (via the myotome), dorsal dermis, and brown fat. Present from E8.5 through E10.0, it maintains an epithelial sheet of proliferating precursors whose dorsomedial and ventrolateral lips progressively delaminate to seed myogenic and migratory muscle progenitor populations throughout the body wall and limb buds.

topLinks.explanation: Dermomyotome and sclerotome are the dorsal and ventral compartments of the somite, both derived from a common segmented paraxial mesoderm/somite progenitor that partitions under opposing dorsal Wnt/BMP-antagonist and ventral Shh (notochord/floor-plate) signals.

The myotome is directly derived from the dermomyotome, as Pax3+ myogenic progenitors delaminate from the dorsomedial and ventrolateral lips of the dermomyotome to form the differentiating myotome, so they share a direct progenitor-progeny somitic lineage.

The hypaxial myogenic progenitors delaminate directly from the ventrolateral lip of the dermomyotome (the Pax3+ somitic dermomyotome), so both cell types derive from the same paraxial-mesoderm/dermomyotome progenitor pool.

Nascent somites, which bud from paraxial/presomitic mesoderm, directly compartmentalize into the dorsal dermomyotome (and ventral sclerotome), so the dermomyotome is an immediate descendant of the somite and both derive from the same paraxial mesoderm progenitor pool.

Both derive from adjacent mediolateral domains of nascent trunk mesoderm ingressing through the anterior/mid primitive streak (fed by the caudal NMP/posterior progenitor pool), so the dermomyotome (dorsal paraxial/somite derivative) and the immediately lateral intermediate mesoderm share recently divergent mesodermal progenitors.

type:Head paraxial mesoderm.name: Head paraxial mesoderm
type:Head paraxial mesoderm.description: Head paraxial mesoderm is a mesenchymal cell population derived from the unsegmented paraxial mesoderm anterior to the otic vesicle, contributing to craniofacial connective tissues, muscles of the head, and portions of the skull. Unlike trunk paraxial mesoderm, which segments into somites, head paraxial mesoderm remains unsegmented and gives rise to much of the cranial musculature and skeletal elements of the face and branchial arches during E8.5–E10.0.

topLinks.explanation: Periocular mesoderm arises largely from cranial (head) paraxial mesoderm, so both cell types descend from the same anterior paraxial mesodermal progenitor pool emerging from the anterior primitive streak/cranial mesenchyme.

Both are cranial mesoderm derivatives that emerge together from the anterior primitive streak/prechordal-to-anterior mesendoderm, sharing a common cranial (head) mesoderm progenitor pool before segregating into paraxial (somitomeric) versus pharyngeal/splanchnic populations.

Both cell types derive from nascent mesoderm ingressing through the anterior primitive streak, and cranial/head paraxial mesoderm is a documented source of angioblasts that give rise to head endothelium, so they share a common paraxial-mesodermal progenitor pool.

Both derive from anterior/cranial mesoderm of the cardiopharyngeal field, where the second heart field and head paraxial (branchiomeric muscle) progenitors share a common Isl1+/Tbx1+ pharyngeal mesoderm origin.

Both cell types are paraxial mesoderm derivatives arising from the anterior primitive streak: head paraxial mesoderm is the unsegmented cranial paraxial mesoderm while sclerotome is the ventromedial somite compartment, so they share a common paraxial mesoderm progenitor pool.

type:Hypaxial myogenic progenitor.name: Hypaxial myogenic progenitor
type:Hypaxial myogenic progenitor.description: Hypaxial myogenic progenitors are migratory muscle precursor cells that delaminate from the hypaxial dermomyotome of somites and travel to distant sites—including the limb buds, body wall, diaphragm, and tongue—where they later differentiate into skeletal muscle. Arising from paraxial mesoderm between E9.0 and E10.0, these progenitors maintain a proliferative, undifferentiated state during migration and are distinguished from epaxial progenitors (which form the deep back musculature) by their long-range migratory behavior and distinct transcriptional program.

topLinks.explanation: Hypaxial myogenic progenitors (from the ventrolateral dermomyotome) and sclerotome are two compartments of the same somite, both derived from a common paraxial-mesoderm/somite progenitor that partitions into dermomyotome and sclerotome under dorsal (Wnt) versus ventral (Shh) signaling.

The hypaxial myogenic progenitors delaminate directly from the ventrolateral lip of the dermomyotome (the Pax3+ somitic dermomyotome), so both cell types derive from the same paraxial-mesoderm/dermomyotome progenitor pool.

Both cell types derive from the somitic dermomyotome of the paraxial mesoderm, where the ventrolateral (hypaxial) dermomyotomal lip gives rise to hypaxial myogenic progenitors while the same dermomyotome contributes myoblasts to the underlying myotome, so they share a common Pax3+/Pax7+ somitic muscle progenitor pool.

Both cell types descend from the somitic dermomyotome, where Pax3+ progenitors are known to be bipotent for skeletal muscle and endothelium, so hypaxial (limb/body-wall) myogenic progenitors and endothelial progenitors co-emerge from this shared paraxial-mesoderm progenitor pool.

Both cell types are mesodermal derivatives whose progenitors emerge adjacently from the posterior primitive streak/tailbud mesoderm and co-develop in the ventrolateral body wall—where somite-derived (dermomyotomal) hypaxial muscle precursors migrate into somatopleuric lateral-plate mesoderm that forms coelomic mesothelium—reflecting a shared common mesodermal progenitor pool rather than a single defined bipotent cell.

type:Myotome.name: Myotome
type:Myotome.description: The myotome is the muscle-forming compartment of the somite, arising from the dermomyotome as cells delaminate and differentiate into the first skeletal muscle cells of the embryo. Present from E8.5 onward, myotome cells are committed, largely post-mitotic myocytes that express myogenic regulatory factors and begin assembling sarcomeric contractile machinery, laying the foundation for axial and body wall musculature.

topLinks.explanation: Myotome and sclerotome are both direct derivatives of the somite (paraxial/presomitic mesoderm), which partitions into the dorsolateral dermomyotome-derived myotome and the ventromedial sclerotome, so they descend from a shared somitic progenitor pool.

The myotome is directly derived from the dermomyotome, as Pax3+ myogenic progenitors delaminate from the dorsomedial and ventrolateral lips of the dermomyotome to form the differentiating myotome, so they share a direct progenitor-progeny somitic lineage.

Both cell types derive from the somitic dermomyotome of the paraxial mesoderm, where the ventrolateral (hypaxial) dermomyotomal lip gives rise to hypaxial myogenic progenitors while the same dermomyotome contributes myoblasts to the underlying myotome, so they share a common Pax3+/Pax7+ somitic muscle progenitor pool.

Both arise from paraxial mesoderm/somites, where Pax3+ central-dermomyotome progenitors are known to be bipotent for skeletal muscle (myotome) and endothelium, so the two lineages descend from a shared somitic angioblast/myogenic progenitor pool.

Intermediate mesoderm and the myotome (a derivative of the somitic dermomyotome/paraxial mesoderm) both arise from mediolaterally adjacent trunk mesoderm compartments specified from a common posterior/presomitic mesodermal progenitor pool (largely NMP-derived) ingressing through the primitive streak, giving them recent shared ancestry.

type:Nascent somite.name: Nascent somite
type:Nascent somite.description: Nascent somites are the most recently formed epithelial segments of paraxial mesoderm, generated sequentially along the anterior-posterior axis through the segmentation clock during somitogenesis. These transient structures represent the initial epithelialized state of somitic mesoderm before further compartmentalization into sclerotome, dermomyotome, and myotome, which ultimately give rise to the axial skeleton, skeletal muscle, and dermis.
