Their presence from E8.0 through E10.0 reflects the continuous rostral-to-caudal progression of somite formation during this developmental window.

topLinks.explanation: Nascent somites are directly generated by the sequential anterior segmentation of the presomitic mesoderm, so both derive from the same paraxial mesoderm progenitor pool (fed by neuromesodermal/tailbud axial progenitors) in an immediate parent-to-daughter lineage relationship.

Axial progenitors include neuromesodermal progenitors (NMPs) in the caudal epiblast/tailbud that bipotentially generate paraxial (presomitic) mesoderm, which directly segments into nascent somites, so the two share a recent common progenitor pool.

Caudal (sacral) spinal cord and nascent somites are both generated late from the same bipotent neuromesodermal progenitors (NMPs) in the tailbud/caudal lateral epiblast, which co-produce posterior neural tube and paraxial mesoderm.

Nascent somites (paraxial mesoderm) and lumbar (posterior) spinal cord both descend from caudal neuromesodermal progenitors (NMPs) in the tail bud/caudal lateral epiblast, a bipotent Sox2/T(Bra)+ population that continuously feeds both the presomitic mesoderm and the posterior neural tube during axial elongation.

Nascent somites, which bud from paraxial/presomitic mesoderm, directly compartmentalize into the dorsal dermomyotome (and ventral sclerotome), so the dermomyotome is an immediate descendant of the somite and both derive from the same paraxial mesoderm progenitor pool.

type:Periocular mesoderm.name: Periocular mesoderm
type:Periocular mesoderm.description: Periocular mesoderm is a specialized cranial mesenchyme population derived from paraxial mesoderm that surrounds the developing eye. These cells contribute to the extraocular muscles, orbital connective tissues, sclera, and choroid, and play essential roles in anterior eye segment morphogenesis during mid-to-late organogenesis (E8.5–E10.0).

topLinks.explanation: Periocular mesoderm arises largely from cranial (head) paraxial mesoderm, so both cell types descend from the same anterior paraxial mesodermal progenitor pool emerging from the anterior primitive streak/cranial mesenchyme.

Both cell types derive from the anterior cranial/head mesoderm (paraxial and splanchnic head mesoderm, including the cardiopharyngeal field), a contiguous rostral mesodermal pool that supplies periocular mesenchyme around the eye and the core mesoderm of the pharyngeal arches.

Both cell types likely descend from cranial/paraxial head mesoderm, where a common angioblast-plus-mesenchyme progenitor pool gives rise to periocular head endothelium and the surrounding periocular mesenchyme, driving their shared ancestry.

Both cell types likely descend from the early anterior mesoderm that ingresses through the anterior primitive streak during gastrulation—the first heart field arising from anterior splanchnic lateral plate/cardiac crescent mesoderm and the mesodermal component of the periocular mesenchyme from adjacent cranial/paraxial (head) mesoderm—so they share a common anterior mesodermal progenitor pool before splitting into cardiac versus cranial fates.

The juxtacardiac field (anterior lateral plate mesoderm) and periocular mesoderm likely share ancestry because both descend from early anterior/cranial mesoderm that ingresses through the anterior primitive streak during gastrulation—consistent with the cardiopharyngeal-field concept linking anterior heart-forming mesoderm to head/periocular mesenchyme.

type:Pharyngeal mesoderm.name: Pharyngeal mesoderm
type:Pharyngeal mesoderm.description: Pharyngeal mesoderm is the mesodermal population that populates the pharyngeal (branchial) arches of the developing embryo, contributing to craniofacial muscles, connective tissues of the head and neck, and the secondary heart field. Arising from a distinct domain of paraxial/cranial mesoderm, these cells interact with neural crest and pharyngeal endoderm to pattern the arches and are essential for normal craniofacial and cardiac outflow tract morphogenesis. This population emerges at E8.5 as the pharyngeal arches begin to form and expands through E10.0 as successive arches are elaborated.

topLinks.explanation: The second heart field is a sub-population of the anterior pharyngeal (splanchnic) mesoderm, both deriving from the common cardiopharyngeal mesoderm progenitor pool (Mesp1+ anterior mesoderm) that co-generates outflow-tract cardiomyocytes and branchiomeric/pharyngeal muscle, so their shared ancestry reflects direct lineage continuity rather than mere co-emergence.

Both are cranial mesoderm derivatives that emerge together from the anterior primitive streak/prechordal-to-anterior mesendoderm, sharing a common cranial (head) mesoderm progenitor pool before segregating into paraxial (somitomeric) versus pharyngeal/splanchnic populations.

Both cell types descend from the anterior lateral plate mesoderm—specifically the cardiopharyngeal mesoderm field where the juxtacardiac field lies contiguous with the cardiac crescent and pharyngeal (second-heart-field) mesoderm, so they share Mesp1+ anterior splanchnic mesoderm progenitors.

Both cell types derive from the anterior cranial/head mesoderm (paraxial and splanchnic head mesoderm, including the cardiopharyngeal field), a contiguous rostral mesodermal pool that supplies periocular mesenchyme around the eye and the core mesoderm of the pharyngeal arches.

Both derive from the anterior splanchnic/lateral plate mesoderm of the cardiopharyngeal field (Mesp1+ second-heart-field progenitors), where endocardial endothelium and pharyngeal/branchiomeric mesoderm co-emerge from a shared multipotent progenitor pool.

type:Presomitic mesoderm.name: Presomitic mesoderm
type:Presomitic mesoderm.description: Presomitic mesoderm (PSM) is the unsegmented paraxial mesoderm tissue located posterior to the last-formed somite, from which new somites sequentially bud off during body axis elongation. Present from E7.5 through E10.0, the PSM is maintained by active Wnt and Notch signaling gradients that drive the segmentation clock and coordinate periodic somite formation along the anterior-posterior axis.

topLinks.explanation: Axial progenitors (neuromesodermal progenitors in the caudal lateral epiblast/tailbud) are the direct bipotent source of presomitic mesoderm, so the two cell types share ancestry because PSM is continuously generated from this Tbx6+/Sox2+ progenitor pool alongside spinal neural tube.

Nascent somites are directly generated by the sequential anterior segmentation of the presomitic mesoderm, so both derive from the same paraxial mesoderm progenitor pool (fed by neuromesodermal/tailbud axial progenitors) in an immediate parent-to-daughter lineage relationship.

Both derive from bipotent neuromesodermal progenitors (NMPs) in the caudal lateral epiblast/tailbud, which co-generate paraxial (presomitic) mesoderm and posterior/caudal (sacral) spinal cord neurectoderm during axial elongation.

Presomitic (paraxial) mesoderm and lumbar spinal cord both derive from bipotent neuromesodermal progenitors (NMPs) in the caudal lateral epiblast/tailbud, which co-generate posterior paraxial mesoderm and posterior spinal neural tube during axis elongation.

Presomitic (paraxial) mesoderm and thoracic/posterior spinal cord both descend from bipotent neuromesodermal progenitors (NMPs) in the caudal epiblast/node-streak border and tailbud that co-produce paraxial mesoderm and posterior neural tube during axis elongation.

type:Sclerotome.name: Sclerotome
type:Sclerotome.description: Sclerotome is the ventromedial compartment of the somite that undergoes epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and migrates around the neural tube and notochord to form the axial skeleton, including vertebrae, ribs, and intervertebral discs. Emerging from E8.5 onward as somites mature, sclerotome cells become migratory mesenchymal progenitors that eventually differentiate into chondrocytes and osteoblasts, establishing the cartilaginous and bony framework of the vertebral column.

topLinks.explanation: Dermomyotome and sclerotome are the dorsal and ventral compartments of the somite, both derived from a common segmented paraxial mesoderm/somite progenitor that partitions under opposing dorsal Wnt/BMP-antagonist and ventral Shh (notochord/floor-plate) signals.

Myotome and sclerotome are both direct derivatives of the somite (paraxial/presomitic mesoderm), which partitions into the dorsolateral dermomyotome-derived myotome and the ventromedial sclerotome, so they descend from a shared somitic progenitor pool.

Hypaxial myogenic progenitors (from the ventrolateral dermomyotome) and sclerotome are two compartments of the same somite, both derived from a common paraxial-mesoderm/somite progenitor that partitions into dermomyotome and sclerotome under dorsal (Wnt) versus ventral (Shh) signaling.

Both derive from paraxial (presomitic/somitic) mesoderm — sclerotome is the ventral somite compartment, and somite-derived angioblasts are a well-documented source of endothelial progenitors (contributing to the dorsal aorta and body-wall/limb vasculature), so the two share a common somitic progenitor pool.

Both derive from trunk mesoderm that ingresses through the posterior primitive streak/tailbud growth zone, where nascent paraxial mesoderm (which segments into somites and their ventral sclerotome) and the immediately adjacent intermediate mesoderm co-emerge from a shared, spatially contiguous progenitor pool.

type:Allantoic endothelial progenitor.name: Allantoic endothelial progenitor
type:Allantoic endothelial progenitor.description: Allantoic endothelial progenitors are extraembryonic mesoderm-derived cells within the allantois that give rise to the umbilical vasculature and contribute endothelial cells to the developing chorioallantoic placenta. Emerging around E8.0 as the allantois buds from the posterior embryo, these progenitors undergo vasculogenesis to form the blood vessels that will connect the embryonic and placental circulations. Their persistence through E10.0 reflects the ongoing vascular remodeling required as the placenta matures and the umbilical cord elongates.

type:Allantois.name: Allantois
type:Allantois.description: The allantois is an extraembryonic mesodermal appendage that buds from the posterior end of the embryo around E7.5 and elongates across the exocoelomic cavity to fuse with the chorion, forming the chorioallantoic placenta essential for maternal-fetal exchange. It also gives rise to the umbilical vasculature. Its presence across all stages from E7.5 to E10.0 is consistent with the allantois's continuous growth and vascular remodeling during this developmental window.

topLinks.explanation: Both arise from posterior primitive-streak/nascent mesoderm, with the allantois forming as an extraembryonic extension of the same lateral-plate (somatopleuric) mesoderm program that produces somatic mesoderm, giving them a shared posterior-mesodermal progenitor origin.
Both arise from posterior primitive-streak-derived caudal mesoderm — the Tbx4/Isl1-expressing posterior lateral-plate/extraembryonic mesoderm pool that produces the allantois and the hindlimb field.

Both derive from posterior primitive-streak-derived lateral plate/extraembryonic mesoderm, with the allantois emerging as an outgrowth of the same posterior splanchnopleuric (visceral lateral plate) mesodermal progenitor pool that gives rise to splanchnic mesoderm.

Allantois (extraembryonic/posterior mesoderm) and surface ectoderm likely share ancestry because both descend from the caudal/posterior epiblast around the primitive streak, where germ-layer segregation occurs late and a common posterior progenitor pool (proximal-posterior epiblast contributing to allantoic mesoderm and adjacent non-neural surface ectoderm) is retained.

Both likely trace back to the posterior epiblast/primitive streak, where allantois (posterior extraembryonic mesoderm) and epidermal surface-ectoderm progenitors co-emerge from the same caudal region before full germ-layer segregation, giving them shared recent ancestry despite belonging to different germ layers.

subtype:Yolk sac endothelial cell.name: Yolk sac endothelial cell
subtype:Yolk sac endothelial cell.description: Yolk sac endothelial cells line the vasculature of the yolk sac, an extraembryonic membrane derived from mesoderm that serves as the primary site of primitive hematopoiesis and nutrient transport during early mouse development. These cells form the first functional vascular plexus in the embryo, appearing at E8.5 as blood islands remodel into a capillary network, and they persist through E10.0 as the yolk sac vasculature matures and supports circulation between the embryo and extraembryonic tissues.

type:Extraembryonic mesoderm.name: Extraembryonic mesoderm
type:Extraembryonic mesoderm.description: Extraembryonic mesoderm is a mesoderm-derived population that gives rise to the mesenchymal and stromal layers of extraembryonic tissues, including the yolk sac mesothelium, allantois, and chorionic mesenchyme. These cells produce abundant extracellular matrix to provide structural support for the extraembryonic membranes and contribute to the developing vasculature that mediates nutrient and gas exchange between the embryo and maternal environment. Present from E7.5 through E10.0, this population persists as a major stromal compartment throughout early organogenesis.

topLinks.explanation: Both lineages trace to yolk-sac extraembryonic (splanchnic) mesoderm, where blood-island hemangioblast/hemogenic-endothelium progenitors generate the primitive hematopoietic wave—including the first megakaryocytes—so megakaryocytes and their surrounding extraembryonic mesoderm share recent common progenitors.

Endocardium and extraembryonic (yolk-sac) mesoderm both arise from Mesp1⁺ early/posterior primitive-streak mesoderm and specifically share a common pool of early angioblast/hemangioblast endothelial progenitors, so their endothelial descendants retain recent common ancestry.

Both derive from the earliest wave of Mesp1+ nascent mesoderm ingressing through the posterior/proximal primitive streak, where first-wave mesoderm produces extraembryonic (yolk-sac/allantois) mesoderm alongside first-heart-field/juxtacardiac cardiac progenitors from a shared early progenitor pool.

The first wave of tissue macrophages in the mouse arises from primitive/erythromyeloid progenitors in the yolk-sac blood islands, which are themselves derived from extraembryonic (yolk-sac) mesoderm, so the two cell types share a common yolk-sac hemangioblast/hemogenic progenitor origin.

Both derive from early posterior/proximal nascent mesoderm emerging from the primitive streak, and specifically the proepicardium/septum-transversum region that gives rise to the epicardium is contiguous with and lineage-related to the anterior extraembryonic (allantoic/amniotic) mesoderm, likely via a shared Hand1+ juxta-cardiac-field-like mesodermal progenitor pool.

type:Hematopoietic progenitor.name: Hematopoietic progenitor
type:Hematopoietic progenitor.description: Hematopoietic progenitors are multipotent blood precursors that emerge from hemogenic endothelium during definitive hematopoiesis in the mouse embryo. Present from E8.5 to E10.0, these cells arise in the yolk sac, para-aortic splanchnopleura, and aorta-gonad-mesonephros region, and give rise to the full spectrum of myeloid and lymphoid lineages.

topLinks.explanation: Both cell types derive from the same yolk-sac/AGM hematopoietic lineage, with embryonic macrophages differentiating directly from hematopoietic (erythro-myeloid) progenitors, so they share recent common progenitors.

Megakaryocytes are a direct hematopoietic derivative, arising from the same hematopoietic progenitor pool (via the megakaryocyte-erythroid progenitor, MEP) that emerges in the yolk-sac/AGM blood-forming program at this stage, so the two share immediate ancestry within a single blood lineage.

The two likely trace back to bipotent mesendoderm progenitors emerging from the anterior primitive streak during gastrulation, where definitive (foregut/pharyngeal) endoderm and nascent mesoderm — including the anterior lateral-plate/pharyngeal mesoderm that seeds early hematopoietic-endothelial progenitors — segregate relatively late from a shared founder pool.

The statistic is actually negative (norm_value −0.236, z −2.57), a significant DEPLETION of shared ancestry that fits their distinct germ-layer origins — mesodermal hematopoietic progenitors (blood islands/hemogenic endothelium) versus neuroectodermal sacral neural crest — which segregate at gastrulation; a genuinely positive linkage would have no obvious shared progenitor.

Endothelial and hematopoietic progenitors share ancestry because both descend from the bipotent hemangioblast/hemogenic endothelium of the extraembryonic yolk-sac blood islands and lateral plate mesoderm, the classic common origin of blood and vessels.

type:Macrophage.name: Macrophage
type:Macrophage.description: Macrophages are tissue-resident myeloid cells that arise from primitive and definitive hematopoiesis in the mouse embryo, becoming prominent from E8.5 onward as yolk sac-derived progenitors seed embryonic tissues. They function as professional phagocytes critical for tissue remodeling, clearance of apoptotic cells during morphogenesis, and innate immune defense.

topLinks.explanation: Both cell types derive from the same yolk-sac/AGM hematopoietic lineage, with embryonic macrophages differentiating directly from hematopoietic (erythro-myeloid) progenitors, so they share recent common progenitors.

Both are myeloid derivatives of yolk-sac hematopoiesis, arising together from the same erythro-myeloid progenitor (EMP)/early hemogenic endothelial pool that seeds primitive macrophages and megakaryocytes at this stage.

The first wave of tissue macrophages in the mouse arises from primitive/erythromyeloid progenitors in the yolk-sac blood islands, which are themselves derived from extraembryonic (yolk-sac) mesoderm, so the two cell types share a common yolk-sac hemangioblast/hemogenic progenitor origin.

Although hepatoblasts derive from foregut endoderm and E9.5 macrophages from yolk-sac/EMP hemogenic-endothelial (mesodermal) progenitors, their shared linkage likely reflects a common early clonal origin in the posterior epiblast/nascent mesendoderm plus tight spatiotemporal co-emergence in the septum-transversum/hepatic region that seeds the fetal-liver hematopoietic niche.

Both cell types likely descend from posterior/lateral plate mesoderm at the venous pole–yolk sac interface, where the proepicardium (giving rise to epicardium) emerges adjacent to the extraembryonic/yolk-sac hemogenic mesoderm that generates the erythro-myeloid progenitors (EMPs) producing E9.5 primitive macrophages.

type:Megakaryocyte.name: Megakaryocyte
type:Megakaryocyte.description: Megakaryocytes are large polyploid cells of the blood lineage that arise from megakaryocyte-erythrocyte progenitors and are responsible for producing platelets, the anucleate cell fragments essential for hemostasis and wound repair. In the mouse embryo, megakaryopoiesis initiates in the yolk sac during primitive hematopoiesis and later transitions to the fetal liver, consistent with their appearance from E8.5 onward in this dataset.

topLinks.explanation: Both are myeloid derivatives of yolk-sac hematopoiesis, arising together from the same erythro-myeloid progenitor (EMP)/early hemogenic endothelial pool that seeds primitive macrophages and megakaryocytes at this stage.

Megakaryocytes are a direct hematopoietic derivative, arising from the same hematopoietic progenitor pool (via the megakaryocyte-erythroid progenitor, MEP) that emerges in the yolk-sac/AGM blood-forming program at this stage, so the two share immediate ancestry within a single blood lineage.

Both lineages trace to yolk-sac extraembryonic (splanchnic) mesoderm, where blood-island hemangioblast/hemogenic-endothelium progenitors generate the primitive hematopoietic wave—including the first megakaryocytes—so megakaryocytes and their surrounding extraembryonic mesoderm share recent common progenitors.

Because they are germ-layer-distinct (endodermal hepatoblast vs. mesodermal megakaryocyte), their shared ancestry most likely reflects clonal co-emergence from a common anterior/ventral progenitor field where the hepatoblast-inducing ventral foregut endoderm and the hemogenic lateral-plate/septum-transversum mesoderm (source of early EMP-derived megakaryocytes) are spatially and temporally co-specified around E9.5.

Both derive from nascent mesoderm ingressing through the primitive streak, so shared ancestry likely reflects a common early lateral-plate/mesodermal progenitor pool before the hematopoietic (megakaryocyte) and anterior cardiopharyngeal (pharyngeal mesoderm) programs segregate.

type:Primitive erythrocyte.name: Primitive erythrocyte
type:Primitive erythrocyte.description: Primitive erythrocytes are the first red blood cells produced during mammalian embryogenesis, arising from yolk sac blood islands during primitive hematopoiesis. Unlike definitive erythrocytes, they are large, nucleated cells that circulate in the embryonic bloodstream and serve as the primary oxygen carriers during early development, from approximately E7.5 through mid-gestation. Their presence from E8.5 to E10.0 in this dataset is consistent with the known window of primitive erythropoiesis in the mouse.

type:Definitive endoderm.name: Definitive endoderm
type:Definitive endoderm.description: Definitive endoderm is an embryonic germ layer that emerges during gastrulation from the anterior primitive streak and displaces the earlier visceral endoderm to form the outermost epithelial layer of the embryo. Present at E7.5, these cells are the progenitors of the entire gut tube and its derivative organs, including the liver, pancreas, lungs, and thyroid. Definitive endoderm is distinguished from visceral (extraembryonic) endoderm by a distinct transcriptional program centered on key endoderm-specifying transcription factors.

type:Foregut.name: Foregut
type:Foregut.description: The foregut is the anterior segment of the definitive endoderm tube, established during gut tube morphogenesis as the embryo undergoes anterior-to-posterior patterning. Present from E8.5 through E10.0, foregut endoderm gives rise to the thyroid, thymus, lungs, liver, stomach, and dorsal pancreas. It is distinguished from hindgut and midgut endoderm by a distinct transcriptional program driven by anterior signaling gradients.

topLinks.explanation: Both derive from anterior definitive endoderm—the pharyngeal endoderm is regionally the rostral/anterior part of the foregut tube itself, so they descend from the same anterior foregut endoderm progenitor pool.

Hepatoblasts are specified directly from the ventral foregut definitive endoderm (the hepatic diverticulum), so foregut and hepatoblast cells share a recent common progenitor in the anterior endodermal lineage.
Foregut and midgut are adjacent anterior-posterior subdivisions of the same primitive gut tube, both deriving from a common definitive endoderm progenitor pool specified during gastrulation.

Foregut and hindgut are both derivatives of the definitive endoderm, which emerges as a single sheet during gastrulation and is subsequently patterned along the anterior-posterior axis into foregut, midgut, and hindgut, so they share a common endodermal progenitor pool.

Both arise from the Foxa2+ anterior primitive streak/node-derived axial mesendoderm, where early notochord progenitors are transiently intercalated within the definitive (gut) endoderm before delaminating, giving foregut and notochord a shared progenitor pool.

subtype:Pancreatic-biliary progenitor.name: Pancreatic-biliary progenitor
subtype:Pancreatic-biliary progenitor.description: Pancreatic-biliary progenitors are multipotent endodermal cells of the posterior foregut that give rise to the pancreas, gallbladder, and extrahepatic bile ducts. Emerging around E8.5–E9.5 in mouse development, these progenitors occupy a critical branch point where pancreatic and biliary fates diverge under the influence of local signaling gradients. Their presence from E9.0 to E10.0 in this dataset is consistent with the developmental window during which the ventral pancreatic and biliary buds are specified and begin morphogenesis.

subtype:Respiratory progenitor.name: Respiratory progenitor
subtype:Respiratory progenitor.description: Respiratory progenitors are ventral foregut endoderm cells that give rise to the trachea, bronchi, and lung epithelium, first specified around E9.0 in mouse development. This population represents the earliest committed precursors of the respiratory lineage, emerging as a bud from the anterior foregut and expanding through E10.0 as the lung buds undergo branching morphogenesis.

subtype:Thyroid progenitor.name: Thyroid progenitor
subtype:Thyroid progenitor.description: Thyroid progenitors are a specialized population of foregut endoderm cells that give rise to the thyroid gland, the earliest endocrine organ to develop in the mouse embryo. These cells emerge from the pharyngeal floor of the anterior foregut around E8.5–E9.0, forming a midline bud that subsequently descends and bifurcates into the bilobed thyroid primordium by E10.0. They are characterized by expression of key transcription factors required for thyroid fate specification, maintenance of thyroid identity, and production of thyroid hormones in later development.

type:Gut.name: Gut
type:Gut.description: Gut endoderm at E8.0 represents the nascent primitive gut tube forming as the definitive endoderm folds ventrally during embryo turning. At this stage, the gut epithelium is largely unregionalized, comprising a broad population of endoderm-derived cells that will subsequently pattern into foregut, midgut, and hindgut domains as organogenesis proceeds.

type:Hepatoblast.name: Hepatoblast
type:Hepatoblast.description: Hepatoblasts are the bipotential liver progenitor cells of the endoderm lineage that give rise to both hepatocytes and cholangiocytes (biliary epithelial cells). Emerging from the hepatic endoderm around E9.0 in the mouse as the liver bud forms, these cells rapidly proliferate and begin expressing early hepatic functions including serum protein synthesis and lipid metabolism, establishing the fetal liver as a major site of hematopoiesis and metabolic activity.

topLinks.explanation: Hepatoblasts are specified directly from the ventral foregut definitive endoderm (the hepatic diverticulum), so foregut and hepatoblast cells share a recent common progenitor in the anterior endodermal lineage.

Both cell types derive from the anterior/foregut definitive endoderm, with hepatoblasts budding from the ventral foregut and pharyngeal endoderm forming the adjacent anterior foregut, so they emerge from a shared foregut endodermal progenitor pool during gut tube regionalization.

Hepatoblasts (the bipotent hepatocyte/cholangiocyte progenitors budding from the ventral foregut) and midgut both derive from definitive (gut-tube) endoderm and emerge from adjacent domains of the ventral foregut–midgut endodermal sheet, so they share a recent common endodermal progenitor pool.

Both hepatoblasts (derived from ventral foregut endoderm) and hindgut cells originate from the common definitive endoderm sheet laid down during gastrulation, so they share an endodermal progenitor pool despite occupying opposite ends of the anterior-posterior gut axis.

Although hepatoblasts derive from foregut endoderm and E9.5 macrophages from yolk-sac/EMP hemogenic-endothelial (mesodermal) progenitors, their shared linkage likely reflects a common early clonal origin in the posterior epiblast/nascent mesendoderm plus tight spatiotemporal co-emergence in the septum-transversum/hepatic region that seeds the fetal-liver hematopoietic niche.

type:Hindgut.name: Hindgut
type:Hindgut.description: The hindgut is the posterior segment of the embryonic gut tube, arising from the ventral folding of posterior definitive endoderm during embryo turning around E8.5. It gives rise to the distal large intestine, rectum, and contributes to the cloaca and allantois-associated structures. Its appearance at E8.5 and persistence through E10.0 is consistent with the progressive elongation and regionalization of the gut tube during these stages.

topLinks.explanation: Hindgut and midgut are contiguous subdivisions of the primitive gut tube that both arise from a common definitive (posterior/visceral) endoderm progenitor pool during gut morphogenesis, so their shared ancestry reflects a single germ-layer and regional origin.

Foregut and hindgut are both derivatives of the definitive endoderm, which emerges as a single sheet during gastrulation and is subsequently patterned along the anterior-posterior axis into foregut, midgut, and hindgut, so they share a common endodermal progenitor pool.

Both hindgut and pharyngeal endoderm are derivatives of the definitive (gut tube) endoderm, arising from the same anterior-primitive-streak-derived endodermal progenitor pool during gastrulation, so their shared ancestry reflects a common germ-layer origin along the emerging gut tube.

Both hepatoblasts (derived from ventral foregut endoderm) and hindgut cells originate from the common definitive endoderm sheet laid down during gastrulation, so they share an endodermal progenitor pool despite occupying opposite ends of the anterior-posterior gut axis.

Both cell types likely trace back to bipotent mesendoderm progenitors ingressing through the early/anterior primitive streak during gastrulation, where prospective definitive (hind)gut endoderm and cranial paraxial (periocular) mesoderm are spatially intermingled before full germ-layer segregation.

type:Midgut.name: Midgut
type:Midgut.description: The midgut is the central segment of the embryonic gut tube that forms between E8.5 and E10.0 as the lateral endodermal folds close along the anterior-posterior axis. This region gives rise to the distal duodenum, jejunum, ileum, cecum, and ascending colon, and is a major site of nutrient absorption in the mature intestine. During the stages captured here, midgut endoderm is undergoing regionalization, elongation, and the early stages of villus morphogenesis.

topLinks.explanation: Hindgut and midgut are contiguous subdivisions of the primitive gut tube that both arise from a common definitive (posterior/visceral) endoderm progenitor pool during gut morphogenesis, so their shared ancestry reflects a single germ-layer and regional origin.
Foregut and midgut are adjacent anterior-posterior subdivisions of the same primitive gut tube, both deriving from a common definitive endoderm progenitor pool specified during gastrulation.

Hepatoblasts (the bipotent hepatocyte/cholangiocyte progenitors budding from the ventral foregut) and midgut both derive from definitive (gut-tube) endoderm and emerge from adjacent domains of the ventral foregut–midgut endodermal sheet, so they share a recent common endodermal progenitor pool.

Both midgut and pharyngeal endoderm are derivatives of the definitive endoderm sheet that emerges from the anterior primitive streak during gastrulation and subsequently folds into the gut tube, so they share a common endodermal progenitor pool despite occupying different anterior-posterior domains.

Although the first heart field is lateral-plate mesoderm and the midgut is definitive endoderm, both likely descend from a shared bipotent mesendoderm progenitor pool ingressing through the anterior primitive streak during gastrulation, whose daughters partition into anterior cardiac mesoderm and gut endoderm.

type:Parietal endoderm.name: Parietal endoderm
type:Parietal endoderm.description: Parietal endoderm is an extraembryonic endoderm lineage that derives from primitive endoderm and migrates along the inner surface of the trophectoderm in the mouse embryo. Its primary function is the secretion of Reichert's membrane, a thick specialized basement membrane that separates the embryo from maternal tissues and serves as a structural and molecular barrier during early post-implantation development.

type:Pharyngeal endoderm.name: Pharyngeal endoderm
type:Pharyngeal endoderm.description: Pharyngeal endoderm is the epithelial lining of the pharyngeal arches and pouches, a transient series of structures in the developing head and neck region. This tissue serves as a critical signaling center for craniofacial morphogenesis and gives rise to derivatives including the thyroid, parathyroid glands, thymus, and ultimobranchial body. Its appearance from E8.5 onward is consistent with the timing of pharyngeal arch formation in the mouse embryo.

topLinks.explanation: Both derive from anterior definitive endoderm—the pharyngeal endoderm is regionally the rostral/anterior part of the foregut tube itself, so they descend from the same anterior foregut endoderm progenitor pool.

Both cell types derive from the anterior/foregut definitive endoderm, with hepatoblasts budding from the ventral foregut and pharyngeal endoderm forming the adjacent anterior foregut, so they emerge from a shared foregut endodermal progenitor pool during gut tube regionalization.

Both midgut and pharyngeal endoderm are derivatives of the definitive endoderm sheet that emerges from the anterior primitive streak during gastrulation and subsequently folds into the gut tube, so they share a common endodermal progenitor pool despite occupying different anterior-posterior domains.

Both hindgut and pharyngeal endoderm are derivatives of the definitive (gut tube) endoderm, arising from the same anterior-primitive-streak-derived endodermal progenitor pool during gastrulation, so their shared ancestry reflects a common germ-layer origin along the emerging gut tube.

Both the notochord (axial mesoderm) and pharyngeal/foregut endoderm arise from the node and anterior primitive streak during gastrulation, sharing an axial mesendoderm progenitor pool in which notochordal-plate cells transiently intercalate with the definitive endoderm before segregating.

type:Visceral endoderm.name: Visceral endoderm
type:Visceral endoderm.description: Visceral endoderm is an extraembryonic endoderm layer that envelops the egg cylinder in early mouse development, functioning as the primary nutrient-absorptive and metabolic epithelium before the definitive yolk sac and fetal liver mature. It mediates maternal-embryonic nutrient exchange through receptor-mediated endocytosis, synthesizes serum transport proteins and apolipoproteins, and plays critical signaling roles in anterior-posterior axis specification during gastrulation. This population persists from E7.5 through E10.0 as part of the visceral yolk sac endoderm.

type:Axial progenitor.name: Axial progenitor
type:Axial progenitor.description: Axial progenitors are a bipotent stem cell population residing in the caudal lateral epiblast and, later, in the tail bud region that fuels posterior body axis elongation from mid-gastrulation onward. They serve as a long-lived source of both spinal cord neural progenitors and paraxial mesoderm (somite precursors), and their gradual exhaustion determines the final length of the embryonic trunk and tail. Their persistence from E8.0 through E10.0 in this dataset is consistent with their known role in sustaining somitogenesis and spinal cord extension throughout this developmental window.

topLinks.explanation: Axial progenitors (neuromesodermal progenitors of the caudal lateral epiblast/tailbud) are the direct bipotent source of caudal neural tube, so sacral spinal cord neurectoderm is generated from this same Sox2/T-expressing progenitor pool, explaining their strong shared ancestry.

Axial progenitors (neuromesodermal progenitors in the caudal lateral epiblast/tailbud) are the direct bipotent source of presomitic mesoderm, so the two cell types share ancestry because PSM is continuously generated from this Tbx6+/Sox2+ progenitor pool alongside spinal neural tube.

Axial progenitors (neuromesodermal progenitors, NMPs) in the caudal lateral epiblast/tailbud directly generate the posterior neural tube, so lumbar (posterior) spinal cord neurectoderm descends from this same self-renewing progenitor pool.

Axial progenitors include neuromesodermal progenitors (NMPs) in the caudal epiblast/tailbud that bipotentially generate paraxial (presomitic) mesoderm, which directly segments into nascent somites, so the two share a recent common progenitor pool.

Axial progenitors (neuromesodermal progenitors, NMPs) in the caudal lateral epiblast/tailbud are the direct source of posterior/trunk spinal cord neuroepithelium, so thoracic spinal cord cells arise from this same self-renewing progenitor pool during body-axis elongation.

type:Epiblast.name: Epiblast
type:Epiblast.description: The epiblast is the pluripotent epithelial tissue of the early post-implantation embryo that gives rise to all somatic cell lineages and the germline. At E7.5, epiblast cells are actively undergoing gastrulation, with subsets delaminating through the primitive streak to form mesoderm and definitive endoderm, while the remaining epiblast retains pluripotency and contributes to the ectoderm.

type:Primitive streak.name: Primitive streak
type:Primitive streak.description: The primitive streak is a transient embryonic structure that forms at the posterior end of the epiblast during gastrulation, serving as the site where epiblast cells undergo epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition to ingress and form the mesoderm and definitive endoderm germ layers. Present at E7.5–E8.0, it is the organizing center for body axis specification and is essential for establishing the anterior-posterior polarity of the embryo.

type:Primordial germ cell.name: Primordial germ cell
type:Primordial germ cell.description: Primordial germ cells (PGCs) are the embryonic precursors of the gametes — sperm and oocytes — that carry genetic information to the next generation. Specified from proximal epiblast cells around E6.25–E7.25 in mouse, PGCs migrate through the hindgut endoderm to colonize the genital ridges by ~E10.5, maintaining pluripotency and undergoing extensive epigenetic reprogramming along the way. Their presence across E7.5–E10.0 in this dataset captures the full migratory phase of PGC development.

topLinks.explanation: Both cell types trace back to the posterior proximal epiblast/posterior primitive streak, where PGCs are specified at the base of the allantois and then transit through the posterior definitive-endoderm-derived hindgut, so they share a common posterior progenitor pool and spatiotemporal origin.

Both lineages likely retain a signature of very early epiblast origin — hypothalamic progenitors from the anterior neural plate and PGCs specified from proximal-posterior epiblast around E6.25 — so any shared ancestry reflects a common pre-gastrulation epiblast pool rather than a dedicated shared progenitor, and with only 25 PGCs this weak (indeed negative norm_value) signal is most likely statistical noise.

Both may trace to the posterior primitive streak/proximal-posterior epiblast that generates posterior lateral plate mesoderm (the septum-transversum–derived proepicardium that forms epicardium) and the adjacent extraembryonic/allantoic mesoderm in which primordial germ cells are specified, giving them a shared posterior-mesodermal progenitor origin.

Both lineages likely trace back to the posterior-proximal epiblast/nascent extraembryonic mesoderm at the base of the allantois, where BMP4-induced PGCs are specified immediately adjacent to the angioblasts/hemangioblast-derived mesoderm that gives rise to arterial endothelium, so they co-emerge from a shared posterior primitive-streak progenitor pool.

Both likely trace back to the proximal-posterior epiblast and its early nascent mesoderm transiting the primitive streak—PGCs are specified from BMP4-induced proximal epiblast adjacent to the same posterior mesoderm that also feeds splanchnic/pharyngeal (second heart field) mesoderm, and the two lineages notably share Prdm1/Blimp1 expression, suggesting a common Blimp1+ proximal-mesodermal progenitor pool.
